summary.big_en: The circulatory system carries food and oxygen to every part of the body and takes waste away.

glossary.def: The heart, the blood vessels and the blood working together to move blood round the body.
glossary.example: Its three main parts are the heart, the blood vessels and the blood (p.3).

glossary.def: The organ that pumps blood around the body.
glossary.example: The left side pumps blood with oxygen to the body; the right side pumps blood without oxygen to the lungs (p.4).

glossary.def: The movement of blood round the body along the same pathway again and again.
glossary.example: Blood always moves along the same pathway in the blood vessels (p.5).

glossary.def: The red liquid that flows around the body carrying food and oxygen.
glossary.example: Blood carries food particles and oxygen to all parts of the body (p.4).

glossary.def: The tubes that blood moves through.
glossary.example: There are three kinds: arteries, veins and capillaries (p.4).

glossary.def: The gas the body needs to stay alive.
glossary.example: The heart pumps blood in arteries to the lungs to pick up oxygen (p.5).

glossary.def: A waste gas that the body must get rid of.
glossary.example: Blood picks it up from the body and carries it to the lungs (p.4).

glossary.def: The small beat you can feel under the skin, caused by the pressure of the blood as the heart pumps it.
glossary.example: Two good places to feel it are the neck and the inside of the wrist (p.7).

glossary.def: The push of the blood against the walls of a blood vessel.
glossary.example: The pressure of the blood is what makes your pulse (p.7).

points.t: The circulatory system has three main parts: the heart, the blood vessels and the blood (p.3).
The heart has two sides. The left side pumps blood with oxygen to the body; the right side pumps blood without oxygen to the lungs (p.4).
Blood carries food and oxygen to the body, and picks up waste such as carbon dioxide (p.4).
The kidneys and the lungs are the organs that get rid of waste products (p.4).
Blood always travels the same pathway: heart to lungs, back to the heart, out to the body, back again (p.5).
Your heart beats about 90 times a minute now, and about 70 times a minute when you are grown up (p.7).
The more active you are, the more often the heart beats, because the body needs more food and oxygen (p.7).

summary.big_en: The respiratory system takes oxygen into the blood and gets rid of carbon dioxide.

The ribs protect the lungs, which fill with air like stretchy sponges (p.13).
Breathing in moves oxygen from the air into the blood vessels in the lungs (p.14).
As the body uses up oxygen it makes carbon dioxide, which the blood carries back to the lungs to be breathed out (p.14).
Breathing in makes the chest bigger; breathing out makes it smaller and pushes the air out (p.14).

summary.big_en: Puberty is the stage of life when the body changes so that it will be able to reproduce.

glossary.def: The stage of life when the body changes and becomes able to reproduce.
glossary.example: It usually starts about age 13 in boys and from about age 11 in girls (p.20).

glossary.def: Chemicals made in the body that cause the changes of puberty.
glossary.example: The changes of puberty are caused by hormones (p.20).

glossary.def: The parts of the body used in reproduction.
glossary.example: Boys and girls have different reproductive systems (p.22).

glossary.def: The sex cell made by the male reproductive system.
glossary.example: A sperm joins with an ovum at fertilisation (p.22).

glossary.def: The sex cells made by the female reproductive system; one of them is an ovum.
glossary.example: Ova are released from the ovaries (p.23).

glossary.def: When a sperm and an ovum join together.
glossary.example: Fertilisation is the start of a new living thing (p.23).

glossary.def: The monthly loss of blood from the womb when an ovum is not fertilised.
glossary.example: Menstruation begins during puberty in girls (p.23).

points.t: Puberty does not happen all at once but in stages, and it starts at different ages in boys and girls (p.20).
The first change is a fast growth spurt: boys can grow 10 cm in a year, girls up to 12 cm (p.20).
Both boys and girls grow more body hair and may get oily skin and pimples (p.20).
The changes of puberty are not the same for everyone and do not all happen at the same time (p.20).
Reproduction is part of the life cycle of all living things (p.19).

summary.big_en: Diseases are caused by living things that infect the body. Our defences and good hygiene help keep them out.

glossary.def: Any living thing that lives on or in the body of another living thing.
glossary.example: The fungus that causes ringworm is a parasite (p.25).

glossary.def: The living thing that a parasite infects.
glossary.example: A person with malaria is the host of the parasite (p.25).

glossary.def: A way the body stops itself from being infected.
glossary.example: Skin, acid, mucus and tears are the body's defences (p.26).

glossary.def: Something that blocks the way in.
glossary.example: The skin acts as a barrier to stop germs getting into the body (p.26).

glossary.def: Sticky liquid in the nose and air passages that traps germs.
glossary.example: Mucus in the windpipe traps germs before they reach the lungs (p.26).

glossary.def: Keeping yourself and the things around you clean.
glossary.example: Washing hands with soap and water before eating is good hygiene (p.27).

glossary.def: An animal that spreads a disease without getting the disease itself.
glossary.example: Mosquitoes are the vector for malaria (p.29).

glossary.def: Something you put on your skin to keep insects away.
glossary.example: Insect repellents help prevent bites (p.29).

points.t: Diseases stop our bodies from working properly. The living things that cause them grow and reproduce in or on the body (p.25).
Bacteria can only be seen with a microscope, and not all of them are harmful (p.25).
Viruses are even smaller than bacteria, and all viruses are harmful (p.25).
Some fungi are useful, such as the yeast in bread, but others are parasites that cause disease (p.25).
Diseases spread by body contact and in food, water and air (p.27).
An insect vector does not cause the disease and does not get it; it passes on the parasite when it bites (p.29).
The body has its own defences that stop germs getting in and kill the ones that do (p.26).

summary.big_en: Igneous rocks form when hot magma or lava cools down and turns solid. Cooling slowly deep in the crust makes big crystals; cooling fast at the surface makes crystals too small to see.

glossary.def: The particular shaped structure of a mineral.
glossary.example: The glassy quartz crystals you can see in a piece of granite (p.66).

glossary.def: Made of crystals — the adjective for crystal.
glossary.example: Every igneous rock is crystalline, whether the crystals are big or tiny (p.66).

glossary.def: An igneous rock that has formed from lava cooling down on the surface of the Earth.
glossary.example: Basalt, a black rock (p.65).

glossary.def: A scientist who studies rocks.
glossary.example: In this unit you work as a geologist, sorting rock samples by what you can see in them (p.64).

glossary.def: A rock which comes from magma that has cooled down into solid rock.
glossary.example: Granite and basalt (p.65).

glossary.def: An igneous rock that has formed when magma cools down inside the Earth's crust.
glossary.example: Granite, which reaches the surface once the rocks above it wear away (p.65).

glossary.def: Part of a rock made of different substances with a crystal structure.
glossary.example: Quartz is a mineral made up of silica and oxygen (p.66).

glossary.def: Seeing something with our eyes without the help of a magnifying glass or hand lens.
glossary.example: Granite crystals are large enough to see with the naked eye; basalt crystals are not (p.66).

glossary.def: The process where liquid magma or lava cools down and becomes solid rock.
glossary.example: Lava at the surface solidifies into basalt (p.65).

points.t: Rocks differ from one another because they were formed in different ways. The scientists who study them are called geologists (p.64).
Rocks are sorted into types by what you can see in them. One main colour with grains stuck together means sedimentary; shiny crystals and a spotted look mean igneous (p.64).
Igneous rocks come from magma that has cooled into solid rock. The word 'igneous' means fire (p.65).
Magma that reaches the surface is called lava, and it solidifies into extrusive igneous rock. Basalt is the example in the book (p.65).
Magma that stays inside the Earth's crust solidifies into intrusive igneous rock. Granite is the example, and it appears at the surface only when the rocks above wear away (p.65).
All igneous rocks are made of minerals, and every mineral is a different group of substances. Silica, oxygen, aluminium, magnesium and iron are the commonest substances in the crust (p.66).
All igneous rocks are crystalline, because crystals form as the minerals cool down (p.66).
The slower the magma cools, the bigger the crystals grow. Deep in the crust they grow large enough for us to see; lava at the surface leaves them tiny (p.66).

summary.big_en: Sedimentary rocks are made of small pieces of older rock that were broken up, worn away, carried by rivers and dropped in layers. Fossils are found in them and nowhere else.

glossary.def: A fossil where the whole animal is preserved in minerals.
glossary.example: The ammonites in limestone, whose moulds filled with minerals and hardened (p.75).

glossary.def: To put down or drop.
glossary.example: A river deposits its sediments when it slows down at a sea or a lake (p.71).

glossary.def: To wear down weathered rocks into sediments.
glossary.example: Broken rock erodes the sides and bottom of a river valley (p.71).

glossary.def: The preserved remains of animals and plants in sedimentary rocks.
glossary.example: A dinosaur in limestone, formed about 150 million years ago (p.74).

glossary.def: An impression of the exact shape and size of something.
glossary.example: A dinosaur's footprint in sandstone in Namibia, about 150 million years old (p.75).

glossary.def: To keep something forever.
glossary.example: Minerals take the place of an animal's bones and preserve its shape as rock (p.74).

glossary.def: Very small pieces of rock.
glossary.example: Rivers, ice and wind wear broken rock into sediments (p.71).

glossary.def: A rock made from small pieces of other rock stuck together.
glossary.example: Sandstone, shale and limestone (p.72).

glossary.def: The process where sediments build up in layers on the sea bed or lake bed.
glossary.example: Layer after layer settles on the sea floor and the bottom ones turn to rock (p.71).

glossary.def: To carry.
glossary.example: Rivers transport sediments from the land out to the sea (p.71).

glossary.def: The landform that a river erodes in the rocks, with the river flowing in it.
glossary.example: The sides and bottom of a river valley are worn away by broken rock (p.71).

glossary.def: A process where heat, ice, rain or plant roots break up rocks.
glossary.example: Rainwater dissolves some rocks and plant roots split their surface (p.71).

points.t: Sedimentary rocks are made from small pieces of other rocks stuck together. Those very small pieces are called sediments (p.71).
Weathering breaks rock up where it lies. High and low temperature crack it, rainwater dissolves some of it, and plant roots split its surface (p.71).
Erosion wears the weakened rock down into sediments. Rivers do it, and so do ice and wind (p.71).
Rivers carry sediments away and drop them where the water slows at a sea or lake. That dropping and building up of layers is sedimentation (p.71).
Sedimentary rocks always form in layers, and that is how you recognise one (p.71).
The three commonest sedimentary rocks are sandstone, shale and limestone (p.72).
Sandstone is sand grains stuck together, and most sand is quartz. Quartz resists weathering at the Earth's surface better than anything else (p.72).
Shale is formed of very fine-grained sediments that are softer than sand. It is usually grey, leaves a mark when scratched, and often breaks in your hands (p.72).
Limestone is made from layers of shells of sea animals that died and sank. Chalk is a pure type of limestone (p.72).
Fossils are the preserved remains of animals and plants, and we find them only in sedimentary rocks (p.74).
A fossil can only form if the animal or plant is buried quickly where there is very little air (p.74).
Minerals in the water gradually replace the bones of a buried animal and harden into rock. What is left is a copy of the original animal (p.74).
A mould is the print an animal or plant leaves in the sediments. A cast is made when minerals fill that mould and set solid (p.75).

summary.big_en: Metamorphic rocks are older rocks that heat, pressure or both have changed into something harder and new. The rock cycle shows how the Earth uses its rocks over and over again.

glossary.def: Burying of sediments with many layers of sediments above.
glossary.example: The bottom layer on a sea bed is buried by everything above it and changes into slate (p.81).

glossary.def: A metamorphic rock made from granite; the word is said like 'nice'.
glossary.example: Its crystals look like the ones in granite, but they lie in bands (p.81).

glossary.def: A large intrusion of igneous rock.
glossary.example: Magma rises from the mantle and forms an intrusive igneous mass inside the crust (p.79).

glossary.def: A rock that has been changed by heat or pressure or both heat and pressure.
glossary.example: Marble, which forms when limestone is heated (p.80).

points.t: Metamorphic rocks are existing rocks that have been changed. The word 'metamorphosis' means change (p.79).
Heat melts all the minerals in a rock, and they then form new crystals (p.79).
Huge pressure squeezes a rock so hard that the new rock has lots of thin layers (p.79).
When heat and pressure act together, the new rock gets both different minerals and many layers (p.79).
A rising mass of magma is what heats and squeezes the rock around it. The hot liquid rock pushes the solid rocks aside as it forces its way into the crust (p.79).
Only the rocks in the zone around the igneous mass are changed (p.79).
Sandstone heated turns into quartzite. It still looks like sandstone, but the crystals shine and the rock is much harder (p.80).
Limestone heated turns into marble, which is extremely hard and very shiny. Its colour depends on what was in the original limestone (p.80).
Shale under intense pressure turns into slate, which forms thin layers (p.81).
Granite heated and squeezed turns into gneiss, whose crystals lie in stripes or bands (p.81).
The rock cycle shows how the Earth's rocks are used over and over again, one type turning into another (p.83).
These changes take hundreds of millions of years (p.83).
The rock cycle diagram is a model, so it shows possible orders of events but not scale or time (p.83).
Magma cools to form igneous rock. That rock then has three ways out: weathering and erosion, heat and pressure, or melting (p.84).
Sedimentary rock has two ways out: burial with heat and pressure, or weathering and erosion (p.85).

summary.big_en: Soil is broken-up rock mixed with organic matter, water and air. Loam has the best mixture for growing plants, and what people do to a soil can either keep it that way or spoil it.

glossary.def: A factory-made fertiliser made from chemicals.
glossary.example: It gives plants nutrients, but it does nothing for the feel of the soil (p.92).

glossary.def: What something is composed of, or consists of.
glossary.example: Loam has the best composition for growing plants (p.90).

glossary.def: A natural fertiliser made of dead organic matter such as dead leaves and insects.
glossary.example: Vegetable peels, egg shells, grass cuttings and weeds kept moist in a warm place (p.92).

glossary.def: A soil with a balance of sand, clay and organic matter.
glossary.example: Loam is the soil a gardener wants, because plants grow best in it (p.90).

glossary.def: Living things or things which were alive, such as dead leaves, bits of root and twigs.
glossary.example: A dark colour shows a soil that holds a lot of organic matter (p.89).

glossary.def: Food for plants in the form of organic matter and minerals such as iron and phosphates.
glossary.example: Plants use up the nutrients, so gardeners keep adding compost (p.92).

glossary.def: A factory-made product that kills unwanted insects but also kills the organic matter in the soil.
glossary.example: Farmers spray it on weeds and insects (p.92).

glossary.def: A mixture of broken up rocks, organic matter, water and air.
glossary.example: A layer of it covers most of the rocks on the Earth's surface (p.88).

glossary.def: The feel of a material; for example, rough or smooth.
glossary.example: Rub a pinch between your fingers: rough, smooth, sticky, crumbly, damp or dry (p.88).

glossary.def: Full of water that will not drain through.
glossary.example: Clay soil goes like this because water cannot get away through it (p.90).

points.t: Soil is a mixture of broken-up rock, organic matter, water and air (p.88).
The broken-up rock in soil comes from weathering. A layer of soil covers most of the rocks on the Earth's surface (p.88).
Organic matter is living things or things that were once alive. Dead leaves, bits of root and twigs count, and so do ants and worms (p.88).
Texture is the word for how a soil feels when you rub it between your fingers (p.88).
Different rocks weather into different soils. Sandstone and quartzite give sandy soil, shale gives clay soil, and igneous and metamorphic rocks give a sandy clay soil (p.89).
Sandy soil has large particles with large spaces between them. It feels rough and crumbly, and water drains through it easily (p.89).
Clay soil has very small particles packed tightly, so there is not much air. It feels smooth and sticky, cracks in dry weather and can become waterlogged (p.90).
Loam is a mixture of sand and clay, so its particles are of different sizes. Its organic matter helps it hold water and gives it plenty of nutrients (p.90).
A dark colour shows that a soil holds a lot of organic matter (p.89).
People change the composition of a soil to suit the plants they grow. Sand is added for a plant that needs good drainage, lime for a plant that needs lime (p.91).
Digging or ploughing mixes air into the soil, which the soil needs to stay as it is (p.92).
Soil needs water, so a farmer or gardener must water it when it does not rain (p.92).
Plants use up the nutrients in the organic matter, so compost or artificial fertiliser has to be added regularly (p.92).
Compost feeds the soil and improves its texture; artificial fertiliser gives the same nutrients but not the texture (p.92).
Looking after a soil means keeping its composition the same. When it is not looked after, the composition changes and plants stop growing well (p.92).

experiments.title: Investigate a soil sample
experiments.summary: A tin of soil is spread out on newspaper, and the group works through questions about its colour, stones, particle size, feel, organic matter, animals, air and water.
experiments.result: Spread out on the paper, the sample shows stones, particles of different sizes, dead leaves and sometimes an ant or a worm.

summary.big_en: A food chain shows who eats whom, and its arrows show where the food and its energy go. Most animals eat many foods, so food chains link up into food webs, and less energy is passed on at every link.

glossary.def: Correct and true, more real, without mistakes.
glossary.example: A food web is a more accurate way than a single food chain to show how energy is transferred (p.100).

glossary.def: A drawing that shows the order in which animals eat plants and other animals to get energy.
glossary.example: Bean plant → grasshopper → lizard → hawk (p.102).

glossary.def: A number of linked food chains.
glossary.example: The rainforest food web from Indonesia, where the orangutan, tiger, python and hawk are all linked (p.100).

glossary.def: To show or stand for.
glossary.example: In a food chain, pictures or words represent the plants and animals (p.99).

glossary.def: A living thing that uses the energy from the Sun to make food.
glossary.example: The bean plant at the start of the chain bean plant → grasshopper → lizard → hawk (p.102).

points.t: A food chain shows the order in which animals eat plants and other animals to get energy. It is drawn with pictures or words joined by arrows (p.99).
The arrows show the direction in which the food moves. Food contains energy, so they also show which way the energy is transferred (p.99).
Every food chain starts with a producer and has at least one consumer. Most food chains have more than one consumer (p.99).
Energy always goes from the producer to the consumer, because the consumer eats the producer (p.99).
Most animals eat more than one kind of food, so they belong to more than one food chain. A frog eats worms, flies and beetles, and large frogs even eat small snakes and mice (p.100).
Different food chains that link together form a food web (p.100).
A food web is more realistic than a food chain. It shows every food chain a living thing can be part of in its habitat (p.100).
Producers get their energy from the Sun and use it to make food (p.101).
Each link is the energy source for the next one. The producers' food feeds the herbivores, and the herbivores feed the carnivores that eat them (p.101).
Not all the energy in the food a consumer eats is passed on to the next link in the food chain (p.102).
A carnivore gets only the energy stored in the body of the herbivore it eats. The rest has already been lost from the food chain (p.102).
Energy is lost at each link, so less and less energy reaches the next link along a food chain or food web (p.102).

checklists.title: Where a herbivore's energy from plants goes (p.102)
checklists.note: Only the stored part reaches the carnivore that eats the herbivore.

experiments.title: Draw food chains
experiments.summary: Three sets of pictures are put in the right order and drawn as food chains: a corn plant, snake and mouse; a cabbage, duck, snail and fox; and a pond with pond weed, tadpole, fish, frog and a person.
experiments.result: Each set turns into one chain that starts with its plant, with arrows leading on to the animals that eat.

experiments.title: Explain a food web and draw food chains
experiments.summary: A food web from the rainforests of Indonesia is used to name its producers, herbivores, carnivores and an omnivore, and to pick out food chains with three and four links.
experiments.result: Arrows run into the orangutan from palm shoots, figs, jack fruit and the coconut palm beetle, and out of it to the tiger and the python.

summary.big_en: Some substances, such as pesticides, mercury and microplastics, are toxic to living things. They pass along a food chain every time one living thing eats another, and the ones that never break down build up until they harm the predators at the end.

glossary.def: To build up or increase.
glossary.example: A pesticide that does not break down builds up from 5 units in a bug to 30 units in an eagle (p.106).

glossary.def: The air, water, land and living things around us.
glossary.example: People put harmful substances into the environment, sometimes by accident and sometimes on purpose (p.105).

glossary.def: Very small particles of plastic that make their way into the environment, especially rivers and seas.
glossary.example: They can be toxic in ocean food chains and food webs (p.104).

glossary.def: Chemicals that farmers and gardeners use to get rid of the pests that eat their plants.
glossary.example: Corn sprayed with a pesticide kills the snails that eat its leaves (p.105).

glossary.def: Harmful or poisonous.
glossary.example: Metals such as mercury and cadmium are toxic to living things (p.104).

points.t: Some substances in the environment are harmful, or toxic, to living things. Metals such as mercury and cadmium are examples (p.104).
Microplastics can also be toxic, especially in ocean food chains and food webs (p.104).
People put harmful substances into the environment, sometimes by accident and sometimes on purpose (p.105).
Pesticides kill pests, but they can also kill consumers that are not pests. Butterflies can die from drinking nectar from a sprayed flower (p.105).
A pesticide moves along a food chain each time one living thing eats another. A bird that eats a poisoned snail takes it in, and so does the predator that eats the bird (p.105).
A pesticide may not kill an animal but can still harm it. A bird's bones may get weaker, for example (p.105).
Some toxic substances break down into harmless substances in the soil or water. Others stay in the environment and do not break down (p.106).
Substances that do not break down accumulate in food chains. They harm the predators at the end of the chain most of all (p.106).
Almost all substances that contain mercury are toxic. They can be dangerous in food chains even at very low levels (p.108).

checklists.title: How a pesticide builds up along one food chain (p.106)
checklists.note: Each animal eats several of the one before, so its amount is theirs added together.

I can explain how a pesticide moves along a food chain

watch_out.wrong: Harmful substances in food chains cannot affect humans.

experiments.title: Play a food chain game
experiments.summary: Learners are rice plants, caterpillars, frogs and kingfishers: the rice plants collect paper pesticide 'particles' into cups, then players tag each other with sticky notes and a tagged player empties their cup into the tagger's.
experiments.result: Each group's average number of particles is recorded in a table and a bar graph, one bar for each living thing in the game.

experiments.title: Research information about mercury in food chains
experiments.summary: Research finds out how mercury gets into the environment and into food chains, how it moves through them and why it harms living things.
experiments.result: The answers are presented as a slide show, poster or information sheet that includes a food chain.

summary.big_en: Mass is how much matter is in an object, and it is the same everywhere. Weight is the pull of gravity on that mass, so it changes when gravity changes.

glossary.def: A person who goes into space.
glossary.example: During spacewalks, astronauts hold on to extra handholds and footholds so they do not float away (p.117).

glossary.def: A device to weigh objects in newtons (N).
glossary.example: It hangs by a hook, and the thing you are measuring hangs from a hook at the other end (p.114).

glossary.def: The unit of measure for weight, named after Isaac Newton who explained the force of gravity.
glossary.example: Weight is written in newtons with the letter N (p.113).

glossary.def: Restoring your body to health.
glossary.example: Back on Earth, astronauts re-train their bodies and re-build their strength (p.117).

glossary.def: The amount of attraction on an object caused by gravity, measured in newtons (N).
glossary.example: You would weigh less on the Moon, because the Moon's gravity is weaker than the Earth's (p.113).

glossary.def: A state of having no weight because there is no gravity.
glossary.example: Astronauts inside the International Space Station float and have a feeling of weightlessness (p.116).

points.t: Mass is the amount of matter in an object. It is measured in kilograms (kg) (p.113).
Weight is the force on an object caused by the pull of gravity. Our weight is the pull of the Earth on our mass (p.113).
Weight is measured in newtons (N). Sir Isaac Newton was the first person to explain what forces are (p.113).
In science, mass and weight are not the same thing. Everyday English uses 'weigh' for kilograms, but an amount in kilograms is really a mass (p.113).
An object has the same mass wherever it is. You would have the same mass on the Moon or on Jupiter (p.113).
The smaller the amount of gravity, the lower your weight (p.113).
The amount of gravity depends on the mass of the object that pulls. The Moon has a smaller mass than the Earth, so its gravity is weaker (p.113).
Mass is measured in grams and kilograms on a measuring scale. For example, you measure the flour, sugar and butter for a cake this way (p.114).
Weight is measured in newtons on a forcemeter (p.114).
Measurements that do not fit the pattern should be repeated (p.115).

Astronauts in the Space Station float because they are not pulled in any particular direction. The station is pulled by gravity, but its forward motion just about equals the speed of its fall (p.116).
Weightlessness confuses the sense of 'up and down'. Astronauts find it hard to tell where their arms and legs are (p.116).
In space, calcium from the bones is lost in urine, so bones weaken and break more easily (p.117).
Muscles become weak in space, so astronauts exercise for two hours a day (p.117).
After a typical six-month space mission, astronauts need several months to recover on Earth (p.117).

watch_out.right: Mass is measured in kilograms, but weight is a force measured in newtons (p.113; WB p.61).

experiments.title: Measure the mass and weight of objects
experiments.summary: Objects of different masses are put on a measuring scale one at a time, then hung in a plastic bag from the bottom hook of a forcemeter.
experiments.result: Every object ends up with two numbers in the table: a mass in grams from the scale and a weight in newtons from the forcemeter.

summary.big_en: A force can start an object moving, slow it down, stop it, turn it or squash it. Force diagrams use arrows to show which forces act on an object.

glossary.def: Not moving; staying still in one place.
glossary.example: A ping pong ball lying still on a table is at rest (p.121).

glossary.def: A drawing with arrows that shows the name, size and direction of the forces acting on an object.
glossary.example: You can draw one for a ball rolling across a table into a book (p.122).

points.t: A force acting on an object can change its size as well as its shape, or make it go faster or slower (p.120).
Forces act on objects that are at rest as well as on objects that are moving (p.119).
Forces are drawn as labelled arrows on a force diagram. The arrows show the name, size and direction of each force (p.119).

checklists.title: Five effects of forces (p.121)

items.sign: change the direction an object is moving
change the shape of an object

checklists.note: Try to think of one example from a ball game for each effect.

items.sign: I can describe the five effects of forces
I can explain that forces act on objects at rest
I can draw a force diagram

experiments.title: Investigate and discuss the effects of forces on an object
experiments.summary: A ping pong ball on a table is blown through a straw, rolled into a book, rolled over a table cloth, flicked from person to person and pressed down gently.
experiments.result: The ball starts rolling, stops at the book, rolls more slowly on the cloth, changes direction when flicked and changes shape when pressed.

summary.big_en: Water pushes up on anything in it with a force called upthrust. An object floats when its mass is no more than the mass of water it pushes aside, and its shape can help it do that.

glossary.def: The moving aside of water as a result of upthrust.
glossary.example: Archimedes noticed how the water was displaced when he sat down in his bath (p.125).

glossary.def: A force that pushes up on an object in water or air.
glossary.example: Push a ball down on to water and you can feel the water pushing up underneath it (p.125).

glossary.def: A pattern on a scatter graph where, when one value goes up, the other value also goes up.
glossary.example: As the base of a foil container gets bigger, the number of coins it holds before sinking also goes up (p.128, p.173).

points.t: Two forces act on an object on water: its weight due to gravity, and upthrust (p.125).
Upthrust causes water to be pushed out of the way. Archimedes, who lived in Ancient Greece, discovered this idea of displacement (p.125).
An object floats if its mass is less than, or equal to, the mass of water it displaces (p.125).
An object sinks if its mass is greater than the mass of water it displaces (p.125).
On a force diagram, a floating object has a gravity arrow equal to or shorter than its upthrust arrow. A sinking object has a gravity arrow longer than its upthrust arrow (p.125-126).
A container ship floats because it displaces an even greater mass of water than its own huge mass (p.126).
Mass is not the only thing that affects floating and sinking; the shape of the object matters too (p.127).
Ships are given the most economical shape to carry heavy loads without sinking (p.128).

checklists.title: Base area of a foil container and the coins it held before it sank (p.128)
checklists.note: The same sized coins were used each time. Plot these as a scatter graph.

items.sign: I can name the two forces on an object in water
I can predict whether an object will float or sink
I can draw force diagrams for floating and sinking
I can explain how shape helps a boat carry more

experiments.title: How does mass affect floating and sinking?
experiments.summary: A small plastic container is put on water, then sand is added 10 g at a time, with a float-or-sink prediction written down before each test.
experiments.result: The container floats at first and sinks once enough sand has been added.

experiments.title: How does shape affect floating and sinking?
experiments.summary: Marbles are tested on their own, then placed one at a time in an aluminium foil dish, and then groups shape foil into different 'boats'.
experiments.result: Each foil boat holds a different number of marbles before it sinks, depending on its shape.

summary.big_en: Circuit diagrams use symbols that people all over the world understand. In a series circuit the current has one path; in a parallel circuit each lamp has its own path to the battery.

glossary.def: A diagram of a circuit using conventional symbols for all the components.
glossary.example: Cells, a lamp and a switch drawn as signs instead of pictures (p.131).

glossary.def: A symbol that is recognised all over the world.
glossary.example: A lamp is drawn as a circle with a cross inside it (p.131).

glossary.def: A circuit where there is more than one pathway and each pathway receives the full circuit voltage.
glossary.example: Two lamps, each connected in its own loop to one battery (p.135).

glossary.def: A circuit where the electric current only has one pathway.
glossary.example: A string of coloured lamps used to decorate a tree for a festival (p.134).

glossary.def: A small sign used on a diagram to represent a real thing.
glossary.example: A motor is drawn as a circle with the letter M inside (p.131).

glossary.def: The unit for measuring the strength of electricity, written V.
glossary.example: A cell is labelled 1.5 V and a battery 3 V (p.131).

glossary.def: The strength of electricity needed for an electrical component or appliance to work.
glossary.example: A 3 V buzzer needs a 3 V battery to make it work (p.133).

points.t: A circuit diagram replaces pictures of components with signs. It is much quicker to draw than a picture of the circuit (p.131).
Everybody uses the same circuit symbols, so people all over the world can read a circuit diagram (p.131).
Different components need different strengths of electricity. A buzzer needs a stronger supply than a lamp (p.133).
Two 1.5 V cells joined together make a 3 V battery (p.133).
In a series circuit the electric current has only one path (p.134).
If one lamp in a series circuit does not work, none of the lamps light up. You have to check every lamp to find the faulty one (p.134).
In a parallel circuit each lamp has its own circuit with the battery (p.135).
If one lamp in a parallel circuit burns out, the rest stay alight (p.135).
Each pathway in a parallel circuit receives the full circuit voltage (p.135).

I can choose components for a circuit

experiments.title: Build circuits with different components
experiments.summary: Groups choose components and build a circuit with a cell, a lamp and a switch, and another with a 3 V battery, a switch and a buzzer, predicting before each one.
experiments.result: The lamp circuit runs on one 1.5 V cell, and the buzzer circuit runs on the 3 V battery.

experiments.title: Make and compare a series circuit and a parallel circuit
experiments.summary: Two lamps are connected to a 3 V battery, first in series and then in parallel; the brightness is compared and then one lamp is unscrewed from each circuit.
experiments.result: With one lamp unscrewed, the other lamp goes out in the series circuit but stays lit in the parallel circuit.

summary.big_en: Mirrors and still water bounce light back, and light leaves a mirror at the same angle as it arrives. A periscope uses two mirrors so you can see over things in your way.

glossary.def: The space between two lines that meet at a surface, measured in degrees.
glossary.example: A ball bounced away from you at an angle leaves the floor at the same angle (p.144).

glossary.def: The ray of light that arrives at the mirror.
glossary.example: In a ray diagram, the arrow pointing in towards the mirror (p.144).

glossary.def: The reflection of something in a mirror.
glossary.example: The reflection of your face that you see in a plane mirror (p.143).

glossary.def: A line drawn at right angles (90°) to the surface of the mirror.
glossary.example: In a ray diagram it stands straight up from the point where the ray meets the mirror (p.144).

glossary.def: A device that uses mirrors so that you can see things that are otherwise out of sight.
glossary.example: People at the back of a golf crowd hold periscopes to see over the heads in front (p.146).

glossary.def: A flat mirror, rather than a mirror with a curved surface.
glossary.example: The flat mirror you look into to see your own face (p.143).

glossary.def: The ray of light that reflects off the mirror.
glossary.example: In a ray diagram, the arrow pointing away from the mirror (p.144).

points.t: Smooth, polished surfaces like mirrors are very good at reflecting light. Clear, still water, such as a lake, reflects light well too (p.143).
When you see your face in a mirror, you are seeing light from your face reflecting off the mirror. That reflection is your mirror image (p.143).
We assume light reaching our eyes has come in a straight line from the object. So reflected light makes a second version of the object: the mirror image (p.143).
Light reflects off a mirror much like a ball bouncing off a hard surface. A ball thrown straight down comes straight back up (p.144).
Light reflects from a mirror at the same angle as it arrives (p.144).
The incident ray and the reflected ray make the same angle with the normal (p.144).
A ray diagram shows how light travels with lines, and arrows for its direction (p.144).
A periscope uses plane mirrors and reflection to let you see over things in the way. People at the back of a crowd use one to see over the heads in front (p.146).
The two mirrors in a periscope are set at 45°. The top mirror faces down and the bottom mirror faces up (p.147).
Light reflects off the top mirror, travels down the periscope, then reflects off the bottom mirror into your eyes (p.148).

items.sign: I can describe how light reflects from a plane mirror
I can label a ray diagram for a mirror
I can explain what a mirror image is
I can explain how a periscope works

experiments.title: Demonstrate how light travels when it reflects
experiments.summary: A flashlight is covered with black plastic that has a pin hole in it, so it gives a thin ray of light. In a darkened room the ray is shone at an upright mirror from different angles, and you watch where it lands on white paper.
experiments.result: Every time, the ray leaves the mirror on the other side of the normal at the same angle it came in.

experiments.title: Make and test a periscope
experiments.summary: Two small plane mirrors are slid into slits cut at 45° near the top and bottom of a tall carton. A window is cut in front of each mirror, on opposite sides of the box.
experiments.result: Looking into the bottom window, you see what is in front of the top window, higher up.

summary.big_en: Light bends when it passes from one material into another, and that can trick our eyes. Lenses and prisms use this bending to make things look bigger or to split white light into colours.

glossary.def: To meet or come together.
glossary.example: Rays that pass through a convex lens bend inward and converge just beyond it (p.152).

glossary.def: A lens with a bulging shape, which makes things look bigger.
glossary.example: A magnifying glass (p.151-152).

glossary.def: The point where rays of light converge.
glossary.example: The point just beyond a convex lens where the bent rays meet (p.152).

glossary.def: A transparent material, such as glass, Perspex or plastic, with at least one curved surface.
glossary.example: Our eyes have lenses in them (p.151).

glossary.def: A material such as air, water or glass.
glossary.example: Light from a fish in a pond passes through two mediums, water and then air (p.150).

glossary.def: Something our eyes see but which is not real.
glossary.example: A pencil standing in a glass of water looks bent (p.151).

glossary.def: A triangular block of glass or clear plastic.
glossary.example: A glass prism splits a narrow ray of white light into colours (p.153).

glossary.def: An arch of colours formed when sunlight is refracted as it passes from the air into raindrops.
glossary.example: A coloured arc in the sky when it is sunny and raining at the same time (p.153).

glossary.def: The bending of light.
glossary.example: Light from a fish bends as it goes from the water into the air (p.150).

glossary.def: Bends, said of light passing from one medium into another.
glossary.example: Sunlight refracts as it passes from the air into a raindrop (p.154).

points.t: Refraction is the bending of light. It happens because light travels at different speeds through different mediums (p.150).
A fish in water is not where it seems to be. Its light bends leaving the water, yet we think it came in a straight line from the fish (p.150).
Refraction makes a stone under water look nearer the surface than it really is (p.166).

A lens bends light rays as they pass through it, so objects seen through it look bigger or smaller than they really are. The rays seem to come from a point closer or further away than they do (p.152).
A convex lens makes things look bigger. Its light rays bend inward and meet at the focal point, just beyond the lens (p.152).
Our eyes have lenses; other lenses are made of glass or transparent plastic (p.151).
The lens in your eye brings distant light rays to a focus. Some telescopes have lenses strong enough to see distant planets and moons (p.152).
White light is actually made up of different colours. A narrow ray of it passing through a prism refracts and splits into those colours (p.153).
Each colour refracts at a different angle (p.153).
A rainbow is an optical illusion made when sunlight refracts passing from the air into raindrops. The raindrops act like tiny prisms (p.154).
To see a rainbow it must be sunny and raining at the same time. The Sun has to be behind you and the rain in front of you (p.153).

checklists.title: The colours white light splits into (p.153)

I can explain why a pencil in water looks bent
I can explain what a convex lens does
I can explain how a prism splits white light
I can explain how a rainbow forms

experiments.title: Demonstrate how light travels when it refracts
experiments.summary: You predict what will happen, stand a pencil in a glass of water and look at it from the side and from the top. Then you take it out to check whether it has changed.
experiments.result: In the water the pencil appears to bend, but out of the water it is unchanged.

experiments.title: Make and test a convex lens
experiments.summary: A square of plastic wrap is laid over some printed words, and one drop of water is placed carefully on top of it.
experiments.result: Seen through the water drop, the words look bigger.

experiments.title: Prisms and rainbows
experiments.summary: A flashlight is shone through a small hole in a sheet of card so that a ray of light falls on one side of a prism.
experiments.result: Coloured light comes out of the other side of the prism, and seven colours can be picked out.

summary.big_en: Eight planets move around the Sun, each turning on its axis and orbiting in its own time. The Moon orbits the Earth once a month, and the lit part we see changes shape in phases.

glossary.def: A time period of 24 hours.
glossary.example: Mercury takes 58.7 Earth days to turn once on its axis (p.160).

glossary.def: A time period of 60 minutes.
glossary.example: Jupiter takes 9.8 Earth hours to turn once on its axis (p.160).

glossary.def: A time period of 365¼ days.
glossary.example: Neptune takes 164.8 Earth years to orbit the Sun (p.160).

glossary.def: The shape of the lit-up part of the Moon that we see from the Earth, which changes over its monthly cycle.
glossary.example: A full Moon, when the whole side facing us is lit up (p.161).

glossary.def: The lit-up part of the Moon getting smaller in its monthly cycle.
glossary.example: From full Moon back to new Moon (p.163).

glossary.def: The lit-up part of the Moon getting bigger in its monthly cycle.
glossary.example: From new Moon to full Moon (p.163).

glossary.def: The Sun and the planets, with their moons, that move around it.
glossary.example: Four small planets lie close to the Sun and four much bigger ones lie further away (p.156).

points.t: The Sun is about 500 times larger than the Moon, but they look about the same size to us. The Sun is much further away: about 150 million km, against 390 000 km for the Moon (p.156).
Four small planets lie close to the Sun, then four much bigger planets lie further away (p.156).
Distances in space are huge. Mercury is 60 million km from the Sun, and Neptune is 4500 million km away (p.156).
An ordinary diagram of the Solar System is not drawn to scale. On a scale drawing Neptune would be a kilometre away from the Sun (p.156).
The Earth turns on its axis once every 24 hours, or one day. It orbits the Sun once a year, every 365¼ days (p.159).
Every body in the Solar System makes these same regular movements, not only Earth. Each takes its own time to turn on its axis and to orbit (p.159).
Turning times are measured in Earth days or Earth hours; orbit times in Earth days or Earth years (p.159).
Venus turns on its axis in the opposite direction to most other planets (p.160).
Jupiter and Saturn consist of gases. Uranus and Neptune consist almost entirely of ice (p.160).
Jupiter's biggest moon, Ganymede, is larger than the planet Mercury (p.160).
Earth has one moon, and it takes 29.5 days to orbit the Earth. We call this a month (p.161).
Like Earth, only half of the Moon can be lit up by the Sun at any one time (p.161).
We see all the phases of the Moon in one month, but a full Moon only once (p.161).

summary.big_en: Some changes can be undone and some can never be undone.

glossary.def: A change that alters how a substance looks or feels, without turning it into a new substance.
glossary.example: A change of state, such as ice melting into water (p.50).

glossary.def: A change that can be changed back again.
glossary.example: Solid ice to liquid water, and liquid water back to solid ice (p.50).

glossary.def: A change that cannot be reversed.
glossary.example: Burning a match: the wood changes into a black substance called carbon (p.50).

glossary.def: The substance that dissolves.
glossary.example: The dissolved salt in sea water (p.51).

glossary.def: The substance in which the solute dissolves.
glossary.example: The water in sea water (p.51).

glossary.def: Looking the same throughout.
glossary.example: A solution has a uniform appearance, so you cannot see the solute in it (p.52).

glossary.def: How fast something happens.
glossary.example: Stirring increases the rate at which a solute dissolves (p.53).

points.t: A physical change alters how a substance looks or feels. The substance does not change into a new substance (p.50).
A change is reversible when the substance can be changed back to the way it was (p.50).
Irreversible changes cannot be reversed, and some turn one substance into another. That is a chemical change (p.50).
The solute and the solvent together form a solution. Sea water is salty because there is dissolved salt in the water (p.51).
When a solute dissolves, its particles move between the solvent particles and spread evenly. That is why you cannot see the solute afterwards (p.52).
Stirring increases the rate at which a solute dissolves. It spreads the solute particles into the spaces between the solvent particles more quickly (p.53).
In a heated solvent the particles gain energy and move faster, so the solute dissolves faster (p.54).

summary.big_en: Different science questions need different ways of finding the answer. Choosing the right type of enquiry is the first step.

glossary.def: Finding information in books, on the internet or in videos, when an investigation is impossible or unsafe to do.
glossary.example: Finding out which other factors, apart from exercise, affect pulse rate (p.10).

glossary.def: Books, the internet and videos that we use to find information when we do research.
glossary.example: Books and websites used to find out how mercury gets into food chains (p.108).

glossary.def: Watching and recording changes as they happen, over minutes, days or even a month.
glossary.example: Recording the shape of the Moon every night for a month (p.ix, p.163).

glossary.def: Naming something from features we recognise.
glossary.example: Naming a blood vessel from the thickness of its wall (p.x).

glossary.def: To sort objects, materials or living things into groups by the ways they are different.
glossary.example: Using a key of 'yes or no' questions to find the type of an igneous rock (p.x).

glossary.def: Observing, recording and analysing data to find a trend or a link between things.
glossary.example: Looking for a pattern linking the mass of an object with its weight (p.x).

points.t: We do research when an investigation is impossible or unsafe to do (p.viii).
Research can compare information from different sources to decide which answer is best. Examples are what affects pulse rate, or harmful substances in food chains (p.viii).
Research also shows that some questions have no answer yet. Scientists do not yet know why gravity only pulls and never pushes (p.viii).
How often we observe depends on the change we are looking at (p.ix).
Some changes happen at once, others take minutes or a month. A gas forms straight away, breathing rate changes within minutes, and the Moon's phases take a month (p.ix).
We classify things by observing how they are different. A key does this with a series of 'yes or no' questions (p.x).
Pattern seeking is used in nature, where the variables cannot easily be controlled (p.x).
Patterns help us find a trend or a link between things. Examples: mass and weight, or a planet's distance from the Sun and the time of its orbit (p.x).

summary.big_en: A test is only fair when just one thing is changed. Then you know that the thing you changed caused the result you measured.

summary.big_en: A table keeps results in order while you collect them. A graph turns the numbers into a picture, so a pattern is easy to see.

glossary.def: A way to record observations and measurements in columns, each with a heading.

glossary.def: A graph with one bar for each thing measured, so the measurements can be compared.

glossary.def: A graph of points joined by a line, showing how a measurement changes.

glossary.def: A graph of dots used to present two sets of data when we think there is a trend between them.

glossary.def: The direction the dots on a scatter graph go in, showing how one value changes as the other changes.

Bar charts show results for separate things, one bar each. Examples are the melting points of solids and friends' pulse rates (p.38, p.33).

summary.big_en: Look for the pattern in your results and check any result that does not fit. Then say what you found out: that is your conclusion.

glossary.def: A link in the results between two things, such as one value going up when another goes up.

glossary.def: Able to be trusted; we check this by repeating measurements or observations.

glossary.example: Sugar dissolves faster in hot water than in cold water (p.54).

The conclusion answers the question you investigated. For example, it says what the effect of temperature on dissolving is (p.54).

Skin, stomach acid, mucus and tears.

flashcards.front_en: Why is a mosquito called a vector?
flashcards.back_en: It spreads the disease parasite when it bites, but does not get the disease itself.
The heart, the blood vessels and the blood working together to move blood round the body.
flashcards.example_en: Its three main parts are the heart, the blood vessels and the blood (p.3).

flashcards.back_en: The organ that pumps blood around the body.
flashcards.example_en: The left side pumps blood with oxygen to the body; the right side pumps blood without oxygen to the lungs (p.4).

flashcards.back_en: The movement of blood round the body along the same pathway again and again.
flashcards.example_en: Blood always moves along the same pathway in the blood vessels (p.5).

flashcards.back_en: The red liquid that flows around the body carrying food and oxygen.
flashcards.example_en: Blood carries food particles and oxygen to all parts of the body (p.4).

flashcards.back_en: The tubes that blood moves through.
flashcards.example_en: There are three kinds: arteries, veins and capillaries (p.4).

flashcards.back_en: The gas the body needs to stay alive.
flashcards.example_en: The heart pumps blood in arteries to the lungs to pick up oxygen (p.5).

flashcards.back_en: A waste gas that the body must get rid of.
flashcards.example_en: Blood picks it up from the body and carries it to the lungs (p.4).

flashcards.back_en: The small beat you can feel under the skin, caused by the pressure of the blood as the heart pumps it.
flashcards.example_en: Two good places to feel it are the neck and the inside of the wrist (p.7).

flashcards.back_en: The push of the blood against the walls of a blood vessel.
flashcards.example_en: The pressure of the blood is what makes your pulse (p.7).

flashcards.back_en: The two organs in the chest that fill with air when you breathe in.
flashcards.example_en: They are like stretchy sponges and are protected by the ribs (p.13).

flashcards.back_en: The air tube that leads from the mouth and nose down to the lungs.
flashcards.example_en: Air from the lungs moves up the windpipe when you breathe out (p.14).

flashcards.back_en: The muscle below the lungs that moves to pull air in and push it out.
flashcards.example_en: It relaxes and moves upwards when you breathe out (p.14).

flashcards.back_en: Moving air in and out of the lungs.
flashcards.example_en: We need to breathe to stay alive (p.13).

flashcards.back_en: How many times you breathe in and out in a minute.
flashcards.example_en: Measured by counting breaths over a set time (p.12).

flashcards.back_en: The stage of life when the body changes and becomes able to reproduce.
flashcards.example_en: It usually starts about age 13 in boys and from about age 11 in girls (p.20).

flashcards.back_en: Chemicals made in the body that cause the changes of puberty.
flashcards.example_en: The changes of puberty are caused by hormones (p.20).

flashcards.back_en: The parts of the body used in reproduction.
flashcards.example_en: Boys and girls have different reproductive systems (p.22).

flashcards.back_en: The sex cell made by the male reproductive system.
flashcards.example_en: A sperm joins with an ovum at fertilisation (p.22).

flashcards.back_en: The sex cells made by the female reproductive system; one of them is an ovum.
flashcards.example_en: Ova are released from the ovaries (p.23).

flashcards.back_en: When a sperm and an ovum join together.
flashcards.example_en: Fertilisation is the start of a new living thing (p.23).

flashcards.back_en: The monthly loss of blood from the womb when an ovum is not fertilised.
flashcards.example_en: Menstruation begins during puberty in girls (p.23).

flashcards.back_en: Any living thing that lives on or in the body of another living thing.
flashcards.example_en: The fungus that causes ringworm is a parasite (p.25).

flashcards.back_en: The living thing that a parasite infects.
flashcards.example_en: A person with malaria is the host of the parasite (p.25).

flashcards.back_en: A way the body stops itself from being infected.
flashcards.example_en: Skin, acid, mucus and tears are the body's defences (p.26).

flashcards.back_en: Something that blocks the way in.
flashcards.example_en: The skin acts as a barrier to stop germs getting into the body (p.26).

flashcards.back_en: Sticky liquid in the nose and air passages that traps germs.
flashcards.example_en: Mucus in the windpipe traps germs before they reach the lungs (p.26).

flashcards.back_en: Keeping yourself and the things around you clean.
flashcards.example_en: Washing hands with soap and water before eating is good hygiene (p.27).

flashcards.back_en: An animal that spreads a disease without getting the disease itself.
flashcards.example_en: Mosquitoes are the vector for malaria (p.29).

flashcards.back_en: Something you put on your skin to keep insects away.

flashcards.front_en: Name the three minerals in granite.
flashcards.back_en: Quartz (glassy), feldspar (white) and mica (black and shiny).
Fire.

flashcards.front_en: Which igneous rock forms from lava at the surface?
flashcards.back_en: An extrusive igneous rock, for example basalt.

flashcards.front_en: Why is most sand made of quartz?
flashcards.back_en: Quartz is very hard, the mineral most resistant to weathering at the Earth's surface.

flashcards.front_en: How old are the ammonite fossils in limestone?
flashcards.back_en: About 240 million years — ammonites no longer exist on Earth.

flashcards.front_en: Why are fossils only found in sedimentary rocks?
flashcards.back_en: A fossil needs quick burial with very little air, which happens where sediments settle in water.
Change.

flashcards.front_en: Which metamorphic rock is made from granite?
flashcards.back_en: Gneiss — its crystals look like granite but lie in bands.

flashcards.front_en: How long do the changes in the rock cycle take?
flashcards.back_en: Hundreds of millions of years.

flashcards.front_en: Name the four things a soil is made of.
flashcards.back_en: Broken-up rock, organic matter, water and air.

flashcards.front_en: Which soil is best for growing plants, and why?
flashcards.back_en: Loam — sand and clay mixed, enough air, holds water and has plenty of nutrients.

flashcards.front_en: What can compost do that artificial fertiliser cannot?
flashcards.back_en: Improve the texture of the soil, not just feed the plants.
The particular shaped structure of a mineral.
flashcards.example_en: The glassy quartz crystals you can see in a piece of granite (p.66).

flashcards.back_en: Made of crystals — the adjective for crystal.
flashcards.example_en: Every igneous rock is crystalline, whether the crystals are big or tiny (p.66).

flashcards.back_en: An igneous rock that has formed from lava cooling down on the surface of the Earth.
A scientist who studies rocks.
flashcards.example_en: In this unit you work as a geologist, sorting rock samples by what you can see in them (p.64).

flashcards.back_en: A rock which comes from magma that has cooled down into solid rock.
An igneous rock that has formed when magma cools down inside the Earth's crust.
flashcards.example_en: Granite, which reaches the surface once the rocks above it wear away (p.65).

flashcards.back_en: Part of a rock made of different substances with a crystal structure.
flashcards.example_en: Quartz is a mineral made up of silica and oxygen (p.66).

flashcards.back_en: Seeing something with our eyes without the help of a magnifying glass or hand lens.
flashcards.example_en: Granite crystals are large enough to see with the naked eye; basalt crystals are not (p.66).

flashcards.back_en: The process where liquid magma or lava cools down and becomes solid rock.
flashcards.example_en: Lava at the surface solidifies into basalt (p.65).

flashcards.back_en: A fossil where the whole animal is preserved in minerals.
flashcards.example_en: The ammonites in limestone, whose moulds filled with minerals and hardened (p.75).

flashcards.back_en: To put down or drop.
flashcards.example_en: A river deposits its sediments when it slows down at a sea or a lake (p.71).

flashcards.back_en: To wear down weathered rocks into sediments.
flashcards.example_en: Broken rock erodes the sides and bottom of a river valley (p.71).

flashcards.back_en: The preserved remains of animals and plants in sedimentary rocks.
flashcards.example_en: A dinosaur in limestone, formed about 150 million years ago (p.74).

flashcards.back_en: An impression of the exact shape and size of something.
flashcards.example_en: A dinosaur's footprint in sandstone in Namibia, about 150 million years old (p.75).

flashcards.back_en: To keep something forever.
flashcards.example_en: Minerals take the place of an animal's bones and preserve its shape as rock (p.74).

flashcards.back_en: Very small pieces of rock.
flashcards.example_en: Rivers, ice and wind wear broken rock into sediments (p.71).

flashcards.back_en: A rock made from small pieces of other rock stuck together.
The process where sediments build up in layers on the sea bed or lake bed.
flashcards.example_en: Layer after layer settles on the sea floor and the bottom ones turn to rock (p.71).

flashcards.back_en: To carry.
flashcards.example_en: Rivers transport sediments from the land out to the sea (p.71).

flashcards.back_en: The landform that a river erodes in the rocks, with the river flowing in it.
flashcards.example_en: The sides and bottom of a river valley are worn away by broken rock (p.71).

flashcards.back_en: A process where heat, ice, rain or plant roots break up rocks.
flashcards.example_en: Rainwater dissolves some rocks and plant roots split their surface (p.71).

flashcards.back_en: Burying of sediments with many layers of sediments above.
flashcards.example_en: The bottom layer on a sea bed is buried by everything above it and changes into slate (p.81).

flashcards.back_en: A metamorphic rock made from granite; the word is said like 'nice'.
flashcards.example_en: Its crystals look like the ones in granite, but they lie in bands (p.81).

flashcards.back_en: A large intrusion of igneous rock.
flashcards.example_en: Magma rises from the mantle and forms an intrusive igneous mass inside the crust (p.79).

flashcards.back_en: A rock that has been changed by heat or pressure or both heat and pressure.
flashcards.example_en: Marble, which forms when limestone is heated (p.80).

flashcards.back_en: A factory-made fertiliser made from chemicals.
flashcards.example_en: It gives plants nutrients, but it does nothing for the feel of the soil (p.92).

flashcards.back_en: What something is composed of, or consists of.
flashcards.example_en: Loam has the best composition for growing plants (p.90).

flashcards.back_en: A natural fertiliser made of dead organic matter such as dead leaves and insects.
flashcards.example_en: Vegetable peels, egg shells, grass cuttings and weeds kept moist in a warm place (p.92).

flashcards.back_en: A soil with a balance of sand, clay and organic matter.
flashcards.example_en: Loam is the soil a gardener wants, because plants grow best in it (p.90).

flashcards.back_en: Living things or things which were alive, such as dead leaves, bits of root and twigs.
flashcards.example_en: A dark colour shows a soil that holds a lot of organic matter (p.89).

flashcards.back_en: Food for plants in the form of organic matter and minerals such as iron and phosphates.
flashcards.example_en: Plants use up the nutrients, so gardeners keep adding compost (p.92).

flashcards.back_en: A factory-made product that kills unwanted insects but also kills the organic matter in the soil.
flashcards.example_en: Farmers spray it on weeds and insects (p.92).

flashcards.back_en: A mixture of broken up rocks, organic matter, water and air.
flashcards.example_en: A layer of it covers most of the rocks on the Earth's surface (p.88).

flashcards.back_en: The feel of a material; for example, rough or smooth.
flashcards.example_en: Rub a pinch between your fingers: rough, smooth, sticky, crumbly, damp or dry (p.88).

flashcards.back_en: Full of water that will not drain through.
flashcards.example_en: Clay soil goes like this because water cannot get away through it (p.90).

flashcards.front_en: What two things do the arrows in a food chain show?
flashcards.back_en: The direction the food moves, and so the direction the energy is transferred.

flashcards.front_en: What does the orangutan eat in the Indonesian rainforest food web?
flashcards.back_en: Palm shoots, figs, jack fruit and coconut palm beetles.

flashcards.front_en: Name three things that happen to a herbivore's energy from plants.
flashcards.back_en: Some keeps it alive, some is stored in its body, and some goes to the surroundings as heat.

flashcards.front_en: Why does less energy reach each next link of a food chain?
flashcards.back_en: Energy is lost at every link; only what is stored in a body is passed on.

flashcards.front_en: Name two toxic metals in food chains.
flashcards.back_en: Mercury and cadmium.

flashcards.front_en: How can a pesticide harm a bird without killing it?
flashcards.back_en: It can make the bird's bones weaker.

flashcards.front_en: What does built-up pesticide do to an eagle's eggs?
flashcards.back_en: It makes the eggshells weak so that they crack.

flashcards.front_en: Which four living things are played in the food chain game?
flashcards.back_en: Rice plants, caterpillars, frogs and kingfishers.

flashcards.front_en: Why does an astronaut weigh less on the Moon?
flashcards.back_en: The Moon has a smaller mass than the Earth, so its gravity is weaker. His mass stays the same.

flashcards.front_en: What does a 10 kg bag of potatoes weigh on Earth?
flashcards.back_en: 100 N. On Earth each kilogram of mass has a weight of 10 N.

flashcards.front_en: How long do astronauts exercise each day in space?
flashcards.back_en: Two hours a day, to try to overcome the weakening of their muscles and bones.

flashcards.front_en: Why do spacecraft have handholds and footholds outside?
flashcards.back_en: So astronauts on spacewalks do not float away.

flashcards.front_en: Name the five effects a force can have.
flashcards.back_en: Make an object move, slow it down, stop it, change its direction, change its shape.

flashcards.front_en: What happens when you blow on a resting ping pong ball through a straw?
flashcards.back_en: The ball starts to move.

flashcards.front_en: What did Archimedes shout in the street, and what does it mean?
flashcards.back_en: 'Eureka!', which is Greek for 'I have solved it!'

flashcards.front_en: Why does a submarine float when its ballast tanks hold air?
flashcards.back_en: Its total mass is less than the mass of the water it displaces.

flashcards.front_en: Which foil container held the most coins before sinking?
flashcards.back_en: The one with the largest base, 16 cm², which held 9 coins.

flashcards.front_en: Which needs a stronger supply of electricity: a lamp or a buzzer?
flashcards.back_en: A buzzer.

flashcards.front_en: Who invented one of the first batteries, and when?
flashcards.back_en: Alessandro Volta, in 1800. His voltaic pile was a pile of copper and zinc discs.

flashcards.front_en: Why are series festival lamps slow to fix?
flashcards.back_en: If one lamp fails none of them light, so you must check every lamp to find the faulty one.

flashcards.front_en: What does each pathway in a parallel circuit receive?
flashcards.back_en: The full circuit voltage.
Smooth, polished surfaces like mirrors, and clear, still water like a lake.

flashcards.front_en: What is the rule for light reflecting off a mirror?
flashcards.back_en: It leaves at the same angle as it arrives; both rays make the same angle with the normal.

flashcards.front_en: Which way do the two periscope mirrors face?
flashcards.back_en: Top mirror faces down, bottom mirror faces up, both set at 45°.
Light travels at different speeds through different mediums, such as water, glass and air.

flashcards.front_en: What does a water drop on plastic wrap do to print?
flashcards.back_en: It magnifies the words — the drop works as a convex lens.

flashcards.front_en: What are the seven colours of white light?
flashcards.back_en: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.

flashcards.front_en: What do you need to see a rainbow?
flashcards.back_en: Sun and rain at the same time, with the Sun behind you and the rain in front.

flashcards.front_en: How far away are the Sun and the Moon?
flashcards.back_en: The Sun is about 150 million km away; the Moon only 390 000 km.

flashcards.front_en: What are the two movements every planet makes?
flashcards.back_en: It turns on its axis, and it orbits the Sun.
Ganymede, which is larger than the planet Mercury.

flashcards.front_en: How long is the Moon's orbit around the Earth?
flashcards.back_en: 29.5 days — one month.

flashcards.front_en: What do we see at new Moon?
flashcards.back_en: No Moon at all — the side facing the Earth is in darkness.
Correct and true, more real, without mistakes.
flashcards.example_en: A food web is a more accurate way than a single food chain to show how energy is transferred (p.100).

flashcards.back_en: A drawing that shows the order in which animals eat plants and other animals to get energy.
A number of linked food chains.
flashcards.example_en: The rainforest food web from Indonesia, where the orangutan, tiger, python and hawk are all linked (p.100).

flashcards.back_en: To show or stand for.
flashcards.example_en: In a food chain, pictures or words represent the plants and animals (p.99).

flashcards.back_en: A living thing that uses the energy from the Sun to make food.
flashcards.example_en: The bean plant at the start of the chain bean plant → grasshopper → lizard → hawk (p.102).

flashcards.back_en: To build up or increase.
flashcards.example_en: A pesticide that does not break down builds up from 5 units in a bug to 30 units in an eagle (p.106).

flashcards.back_en: The air, water, land and living things around us.
flashcards.example_en: People put harmful substances into the environment, sometimes by accident and sometimes on purpose (p.105).

flashcards.back_en: Very small particles of plastic that make their way into the environment, especially rivers and seas.
flashcards.example_en: They can be toxic in ocean food chains and food webs (p.104).

flashcards.back_en: Chemicals that farmers and gardeners use to get rid of the pests that eat their plants.
flashcards.example_en: Corn sprayed with a pesticide kills the snails that eat its leaves (p.105).

flashcards.back_en: Harmful or poisonous.
flashcards.example_en: Metals such as mercury and cadmium are toxic to living things (p.104).

flashcards.back_en: A person who goes into space.
flashcards.example_en: During spacewalks, astronauts hold on to extra handholds and footholds so they do not float away (p.117).

flashcards.back_en: A device to weigh objects in newtons (N).
flashcards.example_en: It hangs by a hook, and the thing you are measuring hangs from a hook at the other end (p.114).

flashcards.back_en: The unit of measure for weight, named after Isaac Newton who explained the force of gravity.
flashcards.example_en: Weight is written in newtons with the letter N (p.113).

flashcards.back_en: Restoring your body to health.
flashcards.example_en: Back on Earth, astronauts re-train their bodies and re-build their strength (p.117).

flashcards.back_en: The amount of attraction on an object caused by gravity, measured in newtons (N).
flashcards.example_en: You would weigh less on the Moon, because the Moon's gravity is weaker than the Earth's (p.113).

flashcards.back_en: A state of having no weight because there is no gravity.
flashcards.example_en: Astronauts inside the International Space Station float and have a feeling of weightlessness (p.116).

flashcards.back_en: Not moving; staying still in one place.
flashcards.example_en: A ping pong ball lying still on a table is at rest (p.121).

flashcards.back_en: A drawing with arrows that shows the name, size and direction of the forces acting on an object.
flashcards.example_en: You can draw one for a ball rolling across a table into a book (p.122).

flashcards.back_en: The moving aside of water as a result of upthrust.
flashcards.example_en: Archimedes noticed how the water was displaced when he sat down in his bath (p.125).

flashcards.back_en: A force that pushes up on an object in water or air.
flashcards.example_en: Push a ball down on to water and you can feel the water pushing up underneath it (p.125).

flashcards.back_en: A pattern on a scatter graph where, when one value goes up, the other value also goes up.
flashcards.example_en: As the base of a foil container gets bigger, the number of coins it holds before sinking also goes up (p.128, p.173).

flashcards.back_en: A diagram of a circuit using conventional symbols for all the components.
flashcards.example_en: Cells, a lamp and a switch drawn as signs instead of pictures (p.131).

flashcards.back_en: A symbol that is recognised all over the world.
flashcards.example_en: A lamp is drawn as a circle with a cross inside it (p.131).

flashcards.back_en: A circuit where there is more than one pathway and each pathway receives the full circuit voltage.
flashcards.example_en: Two lamps, each connected in its own loop to one battery (p.135).

flashcards.back_en: A circuit where the electric current only has one pathway.
flashcards.example_en: A string of coloured lamps used to decorate a tree for a festival (p.134).

flashcards.back_en: A small sign used on a diagram to represent a real thing.
flashcards.example_en: A motor is drawn as a circle with the letter M inside (p.131).

flashcards.back_en: The unit for measuring the strength of electricity, written V.
flashcards.example_en: A cell is labelled 1.5 V and a battery 3 V (p.131).

flashcards.back_en: The strength of electricity needed for an electrical component or appliance to work.
flashcards.example_en: A 3 V buzzer needs a 3 V battery to make it work (p.133).

flashcards.back_en: The space between two lines that meet at a surface, measured in degrees.
flashcards.example_en: A ball bounced away from you at an angle leaves the floor at the same angle (p.144).

flashcards.back_en: The ray of light that arrives at the mirror.
flashcards.example_en: In a ray diagram, the arrow pointing in towards the mirror (p.144).

flashcards.back_en: The reflection of something in a mirror.
flashcards.example_en: The reflection of your face that you see in a plane mirror (p.143).

flashcards.back_en: A line drawn at right angles (90°) to the surface of the mirror.
flashcards.example_en: In a ray diagram it stands straight up from the point where the ray meets the mirror (p.144).

flashcards.back_en: A device that uses mirrors so that you can see things that are otherwise out of sight.
flashcards.example_en: People at the back of a golf crowd hold periscopes to see over the heads in front (p.146).

flashcards.back_en: A flat mirror, rather than a mirror with a curved surface.
flashcards.example_en: The flat mirror you look into to see your own face (p.143).

flashcards.back_en: The ray of light that reflects off the mirror.
flashcards.example_en: In a ray diagram, the arrow pointing away from the mirror (p.144).

flashcards.back_en: To meet or come together.
flashcards.example_en: Rays that pass through a convex lens bend inward and converge just beyond it (p.152).

flashcards.back_en: A lens with a bulging shape, which makes things look bigger.
The point where rays of light converge.
flashcards.example_en: The point just beyond a convex lens where the bent rays meet (p.152).

flashcards.back_en: A transparent material, such as glass, Perspex or plastic, with at least one curved surface.
flashcards.example_en: Our eyes have lenses in them (p.151).

flashcards.back_en: A material such as air, water or glass.
flashcards.example_en: Light from a fish in a pond passes through two mediums, water and then air (p.150).

flashcards.back_en: Something our eyes see but which is not real.
flashcards.example_en: A pencil standing in a glass of water looks bent (p.151).

flashcards.back_en: A triangular block of glass or clear plastic.
flashcards.example_en: A glass prism splits a narrow ray of white light into colours (p.153).

flashcards.back_en: An arch of colours formed when sunlight is refracted as it passes from the air into raindrops.
flashcards.example_en: A coloured arc in the sky when it is sunny and raining at the same time (p.153).

flashcards.back_en: The bending of light.
flashcards.example_en: Light from a fish bends as it goes from the water into the air (p.150).

flashcards.back_en: Bends, said of light passing from one medium into another.
flashcards.example_en: Sunlight refracts as it passes from the air into a raindrop (p.154).

flashcards.back_en: A time period of 24 hours.
flashcards.example_en: Mercury takes 58.7 Earth days to turn once on its axis (p.160).

flashcards.back_en: A time period of 60 minutes.
flashcards.example_en: Jupiter takes 9.8 Earth hours to turn once on its axis (p.160).

flashcards.back_en: A time period of 365¼ days.
flashcards.example_en: Neptune takes 164.8 Earth years to orbit the Sun (p.160).

flashcards.back_en: The shape of the lit-up part of the Moon that we see from the Earth, which changes over its monthly cycle.
flashcards.example_en: A full Moon, when the whole side facing us is lit up (p.161).

flashcards.back_en: The lit-up part of the Moon getting smaller in its monthly cycle.
flashcards.example_en: From full Moon back to new Moon (p.163).

flashcards.back_en: The lit-up part of the Moon getting bigger in its monthly cycle.
flashcards.example_en: From new Moon to full Moon (p.163).

flashcards.back_en: The Sun and the planets, with their moons, that move around it.
flashcards.example_en: Four small planets lie close to the Sun and four much bigger ones lie further away (p.156).

flashcards.front_en: The heart pumps blood through the body. This process is called _____.
flashcards.back_en: circulation

flashcards.front_en: The left side of the heart pumps blood that contains _____ all around the body.
flashcards.back_en: oxygen

flashcards.front_en: Blood vessels that carry blood with food and oxygen away from the heart are called _____.
flashcards.back_en: arteries

flashcards.front_en: Very narrow blood vessels with thin walls that join arteries and veins are called _____.
flashcards.back_en: capillaries

flashcards.front_en: Your _____ is caused by the pressure of the blood as the heart pumps it.
flashcards.back_en: pulse

flashcards.front_en: The lungs are in the chest, where they are protected by the _____.
