flashcards.back_en: ribs

flashcards.front_en: When we breathe in, _____ gas from the air moves into the blood vessels in the lungs.
flashcards.back_en: oxygen

flashcards.front_en: When you breathe in, the diaphragm muscle _____ and moves downwards.
flashcards.back_en: contracts

flashcards.front_en: The number of times we breathe in and out in one minute is called our _____.
flashcards.back_en: breathing rate

flashcards.front_en: The changes that happen during puberty are caused by chemicals in the body called _____.
flashcards.back_en: hormones

flashcards.front_en: In boys, puberty usually starts when they are about _____ years old.
In males, the sex cells are called _____.
flashcards.back_en: sperm

flashcards.front_en: When a sperm and an egg join together, the process is called _____.
flashcards.back_en: fertilisation

flashcards.front_en: In the female reproductive system, the baby develops in the _____.
flashcards.back_en: uterus (womb)

flashcards.front_en: Any living thing that lives on or in the body of another living thing is called a _____.
flashcards.back_en: parasite

flashcards.front_en: The living thing that a parasite infects is called the _____.
flashcards.back_en: host

flashcards.front_en: _____ are even smaller than bacteria, and all of them are harmful.
flashcards.back_en: Viruses

flashcards.front_en: Tears contain a chemical substance that kills some _____.
flashcards.back_en: bacteria

flashcards.front_en: Insects that spread diseases but do not get the diseases themselves are called _____.
flashcards.back_en: vectors

flashcards.front_en: The temperature at which a solid becomes a liquid is its _____ point.
flashcards.back_en: melting

flashcards.front_en: The temperature at which a liquid boils is its _____ point.
flashcards.back_en: boiling

flashcards.front_en: When particles on the surface of a liquid change into a gas, the process is called _____.
flashcards.back_en: evaporation

flashcards.front_en: Most liquids boil only when they are heated, but evaporation can happen at any _____.
flashcards.back_en: temperature

flashcards.front_en: All matter takes up space and has _____.
flashcards.back_en: mass

flashcards.front_en: The transfer of heat energy from one object to another is called _____.
flashcards.back_en: conduction

flashcards.front_en: Metals are good conductors of heat, and _____ is the best conductor of heat.
flashcards.back_en: silver

flashcards.front_en: Of copper, aluminium, graphite, brass and steel, the best conductor of heat is _____.
flashcards.back_en: copper

flashcards.front_en: Substances that are not good conductors of electricity are called _____.
flashcards.back_en: insulators

flashcards.front_en: A change is _____ when the substance can be changed back to the way it was.
flashcards.back_en: reversible

flashcards.front_en: When we burn a match, the wood changes into a black substance called _____.
flashcards.back_en: carbon

flashcards.front_en: The substance that dissolves is the solute, and the substance it dissolves in is the _____.
flashcards.back_en: solvent

flashcards.front_en: Together, the solute and the solvent form a _____.
flashcards.back_en: solution

flashcards.front_en: _____ increases the rate at which a solute dissolves.
flashcards.back_en: Stirring

flashcards.front_en: In a chemical reaction, the substances that react together are called the _____.
flashcards.back_en: reactants

flashcards.front_en: The new substances that form in a chemical reaction are called the _____.
flashcards.back_en: products

flashcards.front_en: When vinegar and bicarbonate of soda react, a _____ is produced.
flashcards.back_en: gas

flashcards.front_en: When clear limewater is mixed with carbon dioxide, it forms calcium _____.
flashcards.back_en: carbonate

flashcards.front_en: Scientists who study rocks are called _____.
flashcards.back_en: geologists

flashcards.front_en: Magma that reaches the surface of the Earth is called _____.
flashcards.back_en: lava

flashcards.front_en: Granite forms from magma inside the Earth's crust, so it is an _____ igneous rock.
flashcards.back_en: intrusive

flashcards.front_en: Basalt forms from lava at the Earth's surface, so it is an _____ igneous rock.
flashcards.back_en: extrusive

flashcards.front_en: The slower the magma cools, the _____ the crystals grow.
flashcards.back_en: bigger

flashcards.front_en: The very small pieces of rock that sedimentary rocks are made from are called _____.
flashcards.back_en: sediments

flashcards.front_en: Heat, rainwater and plant roots break rock up where it lies in a process called _____.
flashcards.back_en: weathering

flashcards.front_en: _____ is made from layers of shells of sea animals that died and sank.
flashcards.back_en: Limestone

flashcards.front_en: The preserved remains of animals and plants in sedimentary rocks are called _____.
flashcards.back_en: fossils

flashcards.front_en: When minerals fill the print left by an animal and set solid, they make a _____.
flashcards.back_en: cast

flashcards.front_en: Existing rocks that have been changed by heat, pressure or both are called _____ rocks.
flashcards.back_en: metamorphic

flashcards.front_en: Limestone that is heated turns into _____.
flashcards.back_en: marble

flashcards.front_en: Shale under intense pressure turns into _____.
flashcards.back_en: slate

flashcards.front_en: Granite that is heated and squeezed turns into _____.
flashcards.back_en: gneiss

flashcards.front_en: The _____ shows how the Earth's rocks are used over and over again.
flashcards.back_en: rock cycle

flashcards.front_en: Soil is a mixture of broken-up rock, organic matter, water and _____.
flashcards.back_en: air

flashcards.front_en: How a soil feels when you rub it between your fingers is its _____.
flashcards.back_en: texture

flashcards.front_en: A soil that is a mixture of sand and clay is called _____.
flashcards.back_en: loam

flashcards.front_en: Water does not drain through clay soil, so it can become _____.
flashcards.back_en: waterlogged

flashcards.front_en: _____ is made from dead organic matter and gives the soil nutrients.
flashcards.back_en: Compost

flashcards.front_en: Every food chain starts with a _____.
flashcards.back_en: producer

flashcards.front_en: The arrows in a food chain show the direction in which the _____ moves.
flashcards.back_en: food

flashcards.front_en: Different food chains that link together form a food _____.
flashcards.back_en: web

flashcards.front_en: Producers get their energy from the _____.
flashcards.back_en: Sun

flashcards.front_en: Energy is _____ at each link, so less reaches the next link in a food chain.
flashcards.back_en: lost

flashcards.front_en: Substances that are harmful or poisonous to living things are called _____.
flashcards.back_en: toxic

flashcards.front_en: Very small particles of plastic that can be toxic in ocean food chains are called _____.
flashcards.back_en: microplastics

flashcards.front_en: Chemicals that kill pests but can also kill other consumers are called _____.
flashcards.back_en: pesticides

flashcards.front_en: Substances that do not break down _____ in food chains.
flashcards.back_en: accumulate

flashcards.front_en: Mass is the amount of _____ in an object.
flashcards.back_en: matter

flashcards.front_en: Weight is a force, so it is measured in _____.
flashcards.back_en: newtons (N)

flashcards.front_en: The Moon has a smaller mass than the Earth, so its _____ is weaker.
flashcards.back_en: gravity
forcemeter

flashcards.front_en: Astronauts floating in the Space Station experience _____.
flashcards.back_en: weightlessness

flashcards.front_en: An object that is not moving is _____.
flashcards.back_en: at rest

flashcards.front_en: On a force diagram, forces are drawn as labelled _____.
flashcards.back_en: arrows

flashcards.front_en: Pressing down gently on a ball at rest changes its _____.
flashcards.back_en: shape

flashcards.front_en: Flicking a moving ball changes the _____ it is moving in.
flashcards.back_en: direction

flashcards.front_en: Water pushes up on an object with a force called _____.
flashcards.back_en: upthrust

flashcards.front_en: The idea of displacement was discovered by _____, who lived in Ancient Greece.
flashcards.back_en: Archimedes

flashcards.front_en: An object floats if its mass is less than, or equal to, the mass of water it _____.
flashcards.back_en: displaces

flashcards.front_en: Mass is not the only thing that affects floating and sinking; the _____ of an object matters too.
flashcards.back_en: shape

flashcards.front_en: A drawing of a circuit that uses symbols instead of pictures is a circuit _____.
flashcards.back_en: diagram

flashcards.front_en: Two 1.5 V cells joined together make a _____ battery.
flashcards.back_en: 3 V

flashcards.front_en: A buzzer needs a _____ supply of electricity than a lamp.
flashcards.back_en: stronger

flashcards.front_en: In a _____ circuit, the electric current has only one path.
flashcards.back_en: series

flashcards.front_en: In a _____ circuit, each lamp has its own circuit with the battery.
flashcards.back_en: parallel
plane

flashcards.front_en: Light reflects from a mirror at the same _____ as it arrives.
flashcards.back_en: angle

flashcards.front_en: The ray of light arriving at a mirror is called the _____ ray.
flashcards.back_en: incident

flashcards.front_en: The _____ is a line drawn at right angles (90°) to the surface of the mirror.
flashcards.back_en: normal

flashcards.front_en: In a periscope, the top mirror has its reflecting surface facing _____.
flashcards.back_en: down

flashcards.front_en: The bending of light is called _____.
flashcards.back_en: refraction

flashcards.front_en: A material such as water, glass or air that light travels through is a _____.
flashcards.back_en: medium

flashcards.front_en: Something our eyes see but which is not real is an _____.
flashcards.back_en: optical illusion

flashcards.front_en: The point where light rays meet after passing through a convex lens is the _____.
flashcards.back_en: focal point

flashcards.front_en: A triangular block of glass or clear plastic that splits white light into colours is a _____.
flashcards.back_en: prism

flashcards.front_en: The Earth turns once on its _____ every 24 hours.
flashcards.back_en: axis

flashcards.front_en: The Earth completes one _____ around the Sun every 365¼ days.
flashcards.back_en: orbit

flashcards.front_en: The Moon takes _____ days to orbit the Earth.
When the lit-up part of the Moon we see is getting bigger, the Moon is _____.
flashcards.back_en: waxing

flashcards.front_en: When the part of the Moon facing the Earth is all in darkness, it is a _____ Moon.
flashcards.back_en: new
Only one variable is changed; all the other variables are kept the same.

flashcards.front_en: Why keep the control variables the same?
flashcards.back_en: So that no other variable can affect the results of the test.

flashcards.front_en: Change, measure, keep the same: which variables are they?
flashcards.back_en: Change the independent variable, measure the dependent variable, keep the control variables the same.

flashcards.front_en: What must a good prediction include?
flashcards.back_en: A reason, based on what you already know about science.

flashcards.front_en: When should you use a scatter graph?
flashcards.back_en: When you expect a trend between two sets of data.
To make the data more reliable, especially a result that does not fit the pattern.

flashcards.front_en: How long does observing the Moon's phases take?
flashcards.back_en: About a month.

flashcards.front_en: When do we do research instead of an investigation?
flashcards.back_en: When an investigation is impossible or unsafe to do.
Finding information in books, on the internet or in videos, when an investigation is impossible or unsafe to do.
flashcards.example_en: Finding out which other factors, apart from exercise, affect pulse rate (p.10).

flashcards.back_en: Books, the internet and videos that we use to find information when we do research.
flashcards.example_en: Books and websites used to find out how mercury gets into food chains (p.108).

flashcards.back_en: Watching and recording changes as they happen, over minutes, days or even a month.
flashcards.example_en: Recording the shape of the Moon every night for a month (p.ix, p.163).

flashcards.back_en: Naming something from features we recognise.
flashcards.example_en: Naming a blood vessel from the thickness of its wall (p.x).

flashcards.back_en: To sort objects, materials or living things into groups by the ways they are different.
flashcards.example_en: Using a key of 'yes or no' questions to find the type of an igneous rock (p.x).

flashcards.back_en: Observing, recording and analysing data to find a trend or a link between things.
flashcards.example_en: Looking for a pattern linking the mass of an object with its weight (p.x).

flashcards.back_en: A test in which we change one variable and keep all the others the same.
flashcards.example_en: Timing how fast a teaspoon of sugar dissolves in 100 ml of hot water and in 100 ml of cold water (p.54).

flashcards.back_en: A factor that can change in an investigation.
flashcards.example_en: Water temperature, the amount of water and the amount of sugar are all variables in a dissolving test (p.viii-ix).

flashcards.back_en: The one variable that we change on purpose.
flashcards.example_en: The water temperature, when testing whether it affects the rate of dissolving (p.viii).

flashcards.back_en: The variable that we measure.
flashcards.example_en: The time it takes the solute to dissolve (p.ix).

flashcards.back_en: The variables that we keep the same.
flashcards.example_en: The amounts of water and solute, and the number of times the solution is stirred (p.ix).

flashcards.back_en: A danger in an investigation that you plan for, so that you can work safely.
flashcards.example_en: Very hot water, which can burn you, when making salt crystals (p.68).

flashcards.back_en: What you think will happen in an investigation, and why, said before you test it.
flashcards.example_en: Before each 10 g of sand is added, saying whether the container will float or sink (p.126).

flashcards.back_en: The observations and measurements collected in an investigation.
flashcards.example_en: The order in which the beads fall off the different materials in hot water (p.44).

flashcards.back_en: A way to record observations and measurements in columns, each with a heading.
flashcards.example_en: Columns for the object, its mass in grams and its weight in newtons (p.115).

flashcards.back_en: A graph with one bar for each thing measured, so the measurements can be compared.
flashcards.example_en: One bar for each living thing's average number of pesticide particles in the food chain game (p.107).

flashcards.back_en: A graph of points joined by a line, showing how a measurement changes.
flashcards.example_en: Breathing rate at rest, after running on the spot and while resting again (p.16).

flashcards.back_en: A graph of dots used to present two sets of data when we think there is a trend between them.
flashcards.example_en: Average air temperature each week against the number of learners off sick (p.171).

flashcards.back_en: The direction the dots on a scatter graph go in, showing how one value changes as the other changes.
flashcards.example_en: More learners were sick in the colder weeks (p.172).

flashcards.back_en: A line drawn through the dots of a scatter graph to make the trend more obvious.
flashcards.example_en: The line through the dots of weekly temperature and number of learners sick (p.172).

flashcards.back_en: A trend where, as one value increases, the other value decreases.
flashcards.example_en: As the temperature went down, the number of learners sick went up (p.173).

flashcards.back_en: When the dots on a scatter graph are scattered and no line of best fit can be drawn.
flashcards.example_en: Dots spread all over the graph with no direction (p.173).

flashcards.back_en: A link in the results between two things, such as one value going up when another goes up.
flashcards.example_en: Toxic particles went from 2 in the algae to 8 in the shrimp and 24 in the small fish (p.111).

flashcards.back_en: Able to be trusted; we check this by repeating measurements or observations.
flashcards.example_en: Testing a substance again when the lamp does not light up, to be sure of the result (p.46).

flashcards.back_en: What you found out in an investigation.
flashcards.example_en: Sugar dissolves faster in hot water than in cold water (p.54).

flashcards.back_en: Something that helps us describe and understand things we cannot see.
flashcards.example_en: A diagram of the circulatory system (p.168).

flashcards.back_en: A solid model that shows the size of a thing and what it looks like inside.
flashcards.example_en: A 3D model of the heart that opens to show the inside (p.168).

flashcards.back_en: A model that shows the real sizes and distances, all made smaller by the same amount.
flashcards.example_en: A ball for the Sun and a lentil for Neptune 250 m away in a field (p.157, p.170).

quiz.stem_en: At what temperature does ice melt?
quiz.why_en: Ice melts at 0 °C (p.36).

quiz.stem_en: What is the melting point of gold?
quiz.why_en: Gold melts at 1064 °C (p.36).

quiz.stem_en: From the Check your progress table, which substance has the LOWEST melting point?
quiz.why_en: Candle wax melts at 60 °C, the lowest in the table (p.62).

quiz.stem_en: Why is the melting point of a substance always lower than its boiling point?

choices.en: Because boiling needs less energy than melting
Because solids are hotter than liquids
Because melting only happens in an oven
Because a substance must be a liquid before it can boil

quiz.why_en: A solid melts into a liquid first; the liquid then needs more energy to boil (p.38 Q5).

quiz.stem_en: Pure water boils at 100 °C. At what temperature does vinegar boil?
quiz.why_en: Vinegar boils at 118 °C (p.36).

quiz.stem_en: What is the difference between boiling and evaporation?

choices.en: Boiling happens through the whole liquid; evaporation only at the surface
Boiling can happen at any temperature; evaporation needs heat

quiz.why_en: In boiling, all the particles gain enough energy; in evaporation only surface particles change to gas (p.36).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these can happen at any temperature, without heating?
quiz.why_en: Evaporation can occur at any temperature; most liquids boil only when heated (p.36).

quiz.stem_en: You heat 100 ml of water and 100 ml of vinegar on the same hotplate. Which boils first, and why?

choices.en: Vinegar — it has the lower boiling point
Water — it has the lower boiling point

quiz.why_en: Water boils at 100 °C, vinegar at 118 °C, so water reaches its boiling point first (p.36, p.38).

quiz.stem_en: Two balloons the same size hang from a balanced ruler. You let the air out of one. What happens?

choices.en: The ruler tips towards the full balloon
The ruler tips towards the empty balloon

quiz.why_en: The full balloon still has the mass of its air, so its side goes down (p.40).

quiz.stem_en: Why can't we usually feel the air around us?

choices.en: Because we only feel air when it is moving

quiz.why_en: "We can't feel air unless it is moving" (p.39). Air is still matter.

quiz.stem_en: A cold metal teaspoon is put into hot tea. After a while the handle feels warm. What is this called?
quiz.why_en: Heat is transferred along the spoon — conduction (p.42-43).

quiz.stem_en: In which cup will tea stay warm the longest?
quiz.why_en: Polystyrene foam is a poor conductor of heat, so heat stays in the tea (p.45 Q4).

quiz.stem_en: Why does food cook faster in the oven in a metal dish than in a glass dish?

choices.en: Metal dishes are lighter than glass dishes are
Glass reflects the oven heat away from the food
Metal dishes are made bigger than glass ones
Metal conducts heat to the food faster than glass

quiz.why_en: Metal is a good thermal conductor; glass is not (p.62 Q2, p.44).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these is a non-metal that CAN conduct electricity?
quiz.why_en: Pencil graphite lights the lamp in the circuit test (p.45-46).

quiz.stem_en: Why are plugs and wire coverings made of plastic or rubber?

choices.en: They are electrical insulators, so electricity cannot reach you

quiz.why_en: Plastic and rubber are electrical insulators (p.61).

quiz.stem_en: Ice melts into water, then the water is put back in the freezer. What kind of change is this?
quiz.why_en: Water can change back to ice — a reversible physical change (p.50).

quiz.stem_en: When a match burns, what does the wood change into?
quiz.why_en: The wood changes into a black substance called carbon (p.50).

quiz.stem_en: Does boiling an egg cause a reversible or irreversible change?

choices.en: Irreversible — the egg cannot go back to raw

quiz.why_en: A cooked egg is a new substance and cannot be changed back (p.50 Q2).

quiz.stem_en: Sort these: which ONE is an irreversible process?
quiz.why_en: Rusting makes a new substance and cannot be reversed; the others are physical changes (p.62 Q3).

quiz.stem_en: In salty sea water, which is the solute and which is the solvent?

choices.en: Salt is the solvent, water is the solute
Salt is the solute, water is the solvent

quiz.why_en: The substance that dissolves is the solute (salt); it dissolves in the solvent (water) (p.51).

quiz.stem_en: Why can't you see the salt after it dissolves in water?

choices.en: The salt sinks to the bottom out of sight
The salt turns into water and stops existing
The salt particles spread evenly between the water particles
The salt floats on the top as a thin film

quiz.why_en: Solute particles spread evenly among the solvent particles — the solution looks uniform (p.52).

quiz.stem_en: Using the particle model, why does sugar dissolve faster in hot water?

choices.en: Heat gives the particles energy so they move faster and spread out
Sugar particles get smaller in heat

quiz.why_en: Heat adds energy; particles move faster and spread the solute through the solvent more easily (p.54).

quiz.stem_en: Will sugar dissolve in a cup of cold water if nobody stirs it?

choices.en: Only if the cup is metal
Yes, but slowly — particles are always moving

quiz.why_en: Particles in matter are always moving, so it dissolves on its own given time (p.54 Q4).

quiz.stem_en: You put vinegar and bicarbonate of soda in a jar. Which are the reactants?
quiz.why_en: The reactants are the substances that react together (p.57).

quiz.stem_en: Your teacher holds a spoon over a burning candle. Which change is a chemical reaction?
quiz.why_en: Melting and hardening wax are reversible; the burning wick forms new substances (p.56).

quiz.stem_en: Limewater mixed with carbon dioxide forms calcium carbonate. Which is the PRODUCT?
quiz.why_en: Calcium carbonate is the new substance formed (p.59 Q2).

quiz.stem_en: You add cornstarch to water with iodine solution and stir. What evidence of a reaction do you see?
quiz.why_en: The colour changes — investigation A (p.58).

quiz.stem_en: You breathe through a straw into limewater. What do you see, and why?

choices.en: It stays clear because nothing at all reacts
It turns cloudy — carbon dioxide in your breath reacts
It turns bright blue because of the oxygen
It bubbles because the straw adds air to it

quiz.why_en: Carbon dioxide reacts with limewater to make cloudy calcium carbonate (p.58-59).

quiz.stem_en: Zara drops a fizzy tablet into water. What evidence of a chemical reaction will she see?
quiz.why_en: Gas is produced — one of the signs of a reaction (p.59 Q3).

quiz.stem_en: Boiling water makes bubbles too. Why is that NOT a chemical reaction?

choices.en: Because no new substance forms — the water just becomes a gas
Because water bubbles are always too small
Because boiling needs a flame and not a reaction
Because the bubbles rise instead of sinking

quiz.why_en: Evidence means a PRODUCT has formed. Boiling is a change of state, not a new substance (p.58, p.36).

quiz.stem_en: Water boils at 100 °C, vinegar at 118 °C and olive oil at 300 °C. Heated equally, which turns into a gas first?

choices.en: Olive oil — it is the thickest
Vinegar — it is in the middle
They all turn to gas together
Water — it has the lowest boiling point

quiz.why_en: The liquid with the lowest boiling point reaches it first (WB p.21).

quiz.stem_en: Why is a wooden spoon good for stirring soup cooking in a pot?

choices.en: Wood makes the soup taste better
Wood is a poor conductor, so heat does not travel to your hand
Wood conducts heat faster than metal

quiz.why_en: Non-metals such as wood are not good conductors of heat (p.44, WB p.24).

quiz.stem_en: Iron and sulfur are mixed and form iron sulfide. Which is the product?
quiz.why_en: The new substance that forms is the product (WB p.33).

quiz.stem_en: Cooking gas burns in oxygen and forms carbon dioxide and water. Which of these is a reactant?
quiz.why_en: Oxygen is one of the substances that react; carbon dioxide and water are the products (WB p.34).

quiz.stem_en: Magnesium is mixed with oxygen: there is a bright white flame and a white powder. Which is the product?
quiz.why_en: The powder is the new substance formed; the flame is evidence, not a product (WB p.34).

quiz.stem_en: Plants use carbon dioxide and water to make oxygen and glucose. Which are the reactants?
quiz.why_en: The substances that react together are the reactants (WB p.35).

quiz.stem_en: True or false: gases do not have mass because we cannot see them.

choices.en: True — you cannot weigh a gas
True — only solids and liquids have mass
False — gases have mass only when cold
False — gases have mass even though we cannot see them

quiz.why_en: All matter takes up space and has mass (p.39); the teacher's slide sets this as false (LMS: Week 7 slides).

quiz.stem_en: True or false: evaporation only happens when a liquid reaches its boiling point.

choices.en: False — evaporation can happen at any temperature
True — it needs the boiling point

quiz.why_en: Evaporation can occur at any temperature (p.36); the slide sets this as false (LMS: Week 7 slides).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these is a property of a substance?
quiz.why_en: A property is something about the substance itself (LMS: Homework 28).

quiz.stem_en: Three substances melt at 25 °C, 80 °C and 150 °C. Which melts first when they are heated together?

choices.en: They all melt at the same time

quiz.why_en: The lowest melting point is reached first (LMS: Homework 28).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these is a reversible change?
quiz.why_en: Melting can be reversed by freezing; burning and cooking make new substances (p.50, LMS: Homework 28).

quiz.stem_en: Which TWO properties does all matter have?

choices.en: It takes up space and it has mass
It is heavy and it is hot
It can be seen and it can be felt

quiz.why_en: All matter takes up space and has mass — including gases like air (p.39).

quiz.stem_en: Which substance is the best conductor of heat?
quiz.why_en: "Silver is the best conductor of heat" (p.44).

quiz.stem_en: A bead is stuck with petroleum jelly onto a metal spoon, a plastic spoon and a glass rod, and all three are stood in hot water. Why does the bead on the metal spoon fall off first?

choices.en: Metal conducts heat best, so the jelly melts first
The bead was stuck on badly

quiz.why_en: Metal conducts heat fastest, melting the petroleum jelly first (p.43-44).

quiz.stem_en: These are values for conducting heat: copper 386, aluminium 237, graphite 168, brass 150, steel 80. Which conducts heat worst?
quiz.why_en: Steel has the lowest heat value in the table, 80 W/m−K (p.47).

quiz.stem_en: These are values for conducting electricity: copper 59, aluminium 37, brass 16, steel 10, graphite 1. Which conducts electricity best?
quiz.why_en: Copper has the highest electricity value, 59 (p.47).

quiz.stem_en: A solution looks the same all the way through. What word describes this?
quiz.why_en: A solution has a uniform appearance (p.52).

quiz.stem_en: Two teaspoons of sugar are put into a cup of coffee, which is then drunk without being stirred. It still tastes bitter. Why?

choices.en: He did not stir, so the sugar had not dissolved

quiz.why_en: Without stirring, the sugar stayed at the bottom (p.53).

quiz.stem_en: Name TWO things that make a solid dissolve faster.

choices.en: Using a bigger jar and more water

quiz.why_en: Stirring and heating both increase the rate of dissolving (p.53-54).

quiz.stem_en: An iron nail is left in a saucer of water. A few days later it has rusted. What is the product of the reaction?
quiz.why_en: The nail had rusted, so rust is the new substance that formed (p.62 Q5).

quiz.stem_en: Vinegar is poured over a ball of wire wool. A reading is taken straight away and again after five minutes. What is being measured?
quiz.why_en: You record the thermometer before and after — a temperature change is evidence (p.59).

quiz.stem_en: How well a substance conducts heat is an example of what?
quiz.why_en: How well a substance can conduct heat is a property of the substance (p.44).

quiz.stem_en: At what temperature does acetone boil?
quiz.why_en: Acetone boils at 50.5 °C (WB p.19).

quiz.stem_en: These are values for conducting heat: silver 420, copper 400, aluminium 250, brass 109, iron 80, stainless steel 15. Which metal conducts heat best?
quiz.why_en: Silver has the highest value, 420 (WB p.24). Note this is a different table from the one on p.47.

quiz.stem_en: These are values for conducting heat: silver 420, copper 400, aluminium 250, brass 109, iron 80, stainless steel 15. Which metal conducts heat worst?
quiz.why_en: Stainless steel has the lowest value, 15 (WB p.24).

quiz.stem_en: Different lengths of graphite are put in a circuit and the lamp brightness is scored 0–5. A 2 cm piece scores 5 and a 12 cm piece scores 0. What does that show?

choices.en: The longer the graphite, the dimmer the lamp
Graphite is not a conductor at all
Longer graphite makes the lamp brighter

quiz.why_en: Brightness falls as the graphite gets longer in their results table (WB p.26).

quiz.stem_en: Sugar is stirred a few times into a cup of warm tea, and afterwards some sugar is still at the bottom of the cup. What two things would have made it all dissolve?
quiz.why_en: Stirring and a higher temperature both increase the rate of dissolving (p.53-54, WB p.30).

quiz.stem_en: Sugar takes 90 s to dissolve at 20 °C, 40 s at 40 °C, 25 s at 60 °C and 15 s at 80 °C. What is the pattern?

choices.en: The hotter the water, the longer it takes
The hotter the water, the less time the sugar takes

quiz.why_en: Their results show the dissolving time falling as temperature rises (WB p.31).

quiz.stem_en: Heat and electricity values: copper 386 and 59, aluminium 237 and 37, brass 150 and 16, steel 80 and 10, graphite 168 and 1. Which substance does NOT fit the pattern that a good heat conductor is also a good electrical conductor?
quiz.why_en: Graphite conducts heat well (168) but electricity very poorly (1) (p.47 Q4).

quiz.stem_en: A lamp has a metal filament, metal support wires, a metal screw-in base and a glass bulb. Which part is NOT an electrical conductor?
quiz.why_en: Glass is an insulator; the metal parts carry the electricity (WB p.23).

quiz.stem_en: What are the three main parts of the circulatory system?

choices.en: The heart, the blood vessels and the blood
The heart, the lungs and the ribs
The blood, the kidneys and the skin
The lungs, the windpipe and the diaphragm

quiz.why_en: The circulatory system has three main parts (p.3).

quiz.stem_en: Which side of the heart pumps blood without oxygen to the lungs?

choices.en: Neither side, the lungs pump it

quiz.why_en: The right side pumps blood without oxygen to the lungs only (p.4).

quiz.stem_en: Where does the left side of the heart pump blood to?
quiz.why_en: The left side pumps blood that contains oxygen all around the body (p.4).

quiz.stem_en: What are the three kinds of blood vessel?
quiz.why_en: There are three kinds of blood vessels (p.4).

quiz.stem_en: Which waste gas does the blood carry away from the body?
quiz.why_en: Carbon dioxide is a waste gas that the body must get rid of (p.4).

quiz.stem_en: Which two organs help the body get rid of waste products?
quiz.why_en: The kidneys and lungs are body organs that help get rid of waste (p.4).

quiz.stem_en: Which veins are the only ones that carry blood containing oxygen?

choices.en: The veins from the body back to the heart
The veins that go from the heart to the body
The veins from the lungs back to the heart
All veins carry blood with oxygen

quiz.why_en: Those are the only veins that carry blood with oxygen (p.5).

quiz.stem_en: About how many times a minute does a child's heart beat?
quiz.why_en: Your heart beats about 90 times a minute, and about 70 when grown up (p.7).

quiz.stem_en: What causes your pulse?

choices.en: The pressure of the blood as the heart pumps it
The muscles of the arm tightening

quiz.why_en: The pulse is caused by the pressure of the blood as the heart pumps it (p.7).

quiz.stem_en: Why does the heart beat more often when you run around?

choices.en: The blood gets thicker when you run
The body needs more food and oxygen
The lungs get smaller when you run
The heart muscle gets tired and slows

quiz.why_en: The more active you are, the more often the heart must beat (p.7).

quiz.stem_en: Which three things make up the respiratory system?

choices.en: Two lungs, the heart, and blood vessels
The nose, the stomach, and the ribs
Two lungs, air tubes, and muscles in the chest
The windpipe, the kidneys, and the diaphragm

quiz.why_en: The human respiratory system contains these parts (p.13).

quiz.stem_en: What protects the lungs?
quiz.why_en: The lungs are in the chest and are protected by the ribs (p.13).

quiz.stem_en: When you breathe in, where does the oxygen go?

choices.en: Into the blood vessels in the lungs
Into the windpipe and stays there
Into the muscles of the chest

quiz.why_en: Oxygen gas from the air moves into the blood vessels in the lungs (p.14).

quiz.stem_en: Where does the carbon dioxide in your breath come from?

choices.en: It comes in from the air you breathe
The body makes it as it uses up oxygen
The lungs make it out of water
The heart makes it from food

quiz.why_en: As your body uses up oxygen, it makes carbon dioxide (p.14).

quiz.stem_en: When you breathe out, what do the ribs and the diaphragm do?

choices.en: The ribs move up and out; the diaphragm moves down
Both the ribs and the diaphragm move down
The ribs move down and in; the diaphragm relaxes and moves up
The ribs stay still; only the diaphragm moves down

quiz.why_en: That is how the chest gets smaller and air is pushed out (p.14).

quiz.stem_en: What is the stage of life called when the body becomes able to reproduce?
quiz.why_en: This stage in your life is called puberty (p.20).

quiz.stem_en: What causes the changes that happen during puberty?

choices.en: Chemicals in the body called hormones

quiz.why_en: These changes are caused by hormones (p.20).

quiz.stem_en: At about what age does puberty usually start in boys?
quiz.why_en: In boys, puberty usually starts at about 13 (p.20).

quiz.stem_en: How much can girls grow in a year as puberty starts?
quiz.why_en: Girls can grow up to 12 cm in a year; boys can easily grow 10 cm (p.20).

quiz.stem_en: What is fertilisation?

choices.en: When a sperm and an ovum join together

quiz.why_en: Fertilisation is when a sperm joins with an ovum (p.23).

quiz.stem_en: What is a parasite?

choices.en: Any living thing that lives on or in the body of another living thing
Any living thing that is too small to see
Any germ that lives in water

quiz.why_en: That is the definition the book gives (p.25).

quiz.stem_en: What do we call the living thing that a parasite infects?
quiz.why_en: The living thing that a parasite infects is called the host (p.25).

quiz.stem_en: Which statement about bacteria and viruses is correct?

choices.en: All bacteria are harmful, but not all viruses are
All viruses are harmful, but not all bacteria are

quiz.why_en: Not all bacteria are harmful; all viruses are harmful (p.25).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these diseases is caused by a fungus?
quiz.why_en: Ringworm and athlete's foot are caused by fungi (p.25).

quiz.stem_en: Yeast used to make bread rise is a fungus. What does that show?

choices.en: Not every fungus is a parasite that causes disease
Bread can give you a disease
All fungi are useful to people
Yeast is really a kind of bacteria

quiz.why_en: Some fungi are useful, but some are parasites that cause disease (p.25).

quiz.stem_en: How does the skin defend the body against disease?

choices.en: It traps germs in sticky mucus
It acts as a barrier that stops germs getting in
It kills germs with a chemical in tears
It kills germs with stomach acid

quiz.why_en: The skin acts as a barrier to stop germs getting into the body (p.26).

quiz.stem_en: What does the acid in your stomach do?

choices.en: It traps germs in the nose
It kills germs in the food we have eaten
It carries germs to the kidneys

quiz.why_en: Acid in the stomach kills germs in food (p.26).

quiz.stem_en: Which defence traps germs in the nose and windpipe?
quiz.why_en: Sticky mucus in the nose and air passages traps germs (p.26).

quiz.stem_en: Diseases spread in four ways. Which list is right?

choices.en: Body contact, food, water and air
Body contact, soil, sunlight and air

quiz.why_en: Diseases can be spread by body contact and in food, in water and in the air (p.27).

quiz.stem_en: Mosquitoes spread malaria but do not get the disease. What are they called?
quiz.why_en: We say the insects are vectors (p.29).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these helps prevent a disease that is spread by insects?
quiz.why_en: Sleeping under bed nets is one of the ways to prevent insect bites (p.29).

quiz.stem_en: In a class survey of 38 answers, 12 people kept the kitchen and toilet clean and 4 washed their hands after working with food. What does that show?

choices.en: Washing hands after food was the most popular method by far
Everyone in the survey used exactly the same method
Nobody in the survey covered their nose when sneezing
Keeping surroundings clean was the most used method and washing hands after food the least

quiz.why_en: 12 was the highest count and 4 the lowest in the survey results (p.28).

quiz.stem_en: What do we call a scientist who studies rocks?
quiz.why_en: Geologists are the scientists who study rocks (p.64).

quiz.stem_en: You find a rock that is one main colour and made of grains stuck together. Which type of rock is it most likely to be?
quiz.why_en: Rocks of one main colour made of grains stuck together are sedimentary rocks (p.64).

quiz.stem_en: Igneous rocks form from which material?

choices.en: the shells of dead sea animals
magma that has cooled and turned solid

quiz.why_en: Igneous rocks come from magma that has cooled into solid rock (p.65).

quiz.stem_en: Lava cools on the surface of the Earth and turns solid. What kind of rock forms?
quiz.why_en: 'Extrusive' means outside the crust, on the surface; basalt forms this way (p.65).

quiz.stem_en: Granite forms from magma that stays inside the Earth's crust. What is granite an example of?
quiz.why_en: 'Intrusive' means inside the crust, and granite is the book's example (p.65).

quiz.stem_en: What is the name of the process where liquid magma or lava cools down and becomes solid rock?
quiz.why_en: Solidification is magma or lava cooling down into solid rock (p.65).

quiz.stem_en: All igneous rocks are crystalline. When do the crystals form?

choices.en: when layers above squash the rock
when plant roots break the rock up

quiz.why_en: Crystals are formed when the minerals cool down (p.66).

quiz.stem_en: A rock has crystals so small that you cannot see them with the naked eye. What does that tell you about how it formed?

choices.en: it cooled slowly deep in the crust
it was never hot at all
it cooled quickly at the surface

quiz.why_en: Lava cools quickly, so the crystals in basalt are too small to see (p.66).

quiz.stem_en: Which three minerals make up granite?
quiz.why_en: The minerals in granite are quartz, feldspar and mica (p.66).

quiz.stem_en: Which two substances is the mineral quartz made of?
quiz.why_en: Quartz is a mineral made up of silica and oxygen (p.66).

quiz.stem_en: Smooth black stones cover the beach of an island with a big mountain in the middle. Are they more likely to be granite or basalt?

choices.en: granite, because the sea has smoothed and polished the stones
basalt, because the mountain is made of crushed sea shells
basalt, because it formed from lava that cooled at the surface
granite, because it formed from magma deep inside the crust

quiz.why_en: Black rock on a volcanic island is basalt, an extrusive igneous rock (WB p.39).

quiz.stem_en: What are sediments?
quiz.why_en: Sediments are very small pieces of rock (p.71).

quiz.stem_en: Rain, ice and plant roots break rocks up where they lie. What is this process called?
quiz.why_en: Weathering is heat, ice, rain or plant roots breaking up rocks (p.71).

quiz.stem_en: A river wears down the sides and bottom of its valley. What is this process called?
quiz.why_en: Eroding is wearing weathered rock down into sediments (p.71).

quiz.stem_en: Where does a river deposit the sediments it is carrying?

choices.en: high up in the mountains where it begins
where it flows fastest over the rocks
where it slows down as it reaches a sea or a lake
in the clouds, when the water evaporates

quiz.why_en: When a river reaches the sea or a lake it flows slowly and drops its sediments (p.71).

quiz.stem_en: What is it called when sediments build up in layers on the sea bed?
quiz.why_en: Sedimentation is sediments building up in layers on a sea bed or lake bed (p.71).

quiz.stem_en: Sediments pile up on a sea floor for millions of years. Which layers turn into rock?

choices.en: the bottom layers, because they are squashed by everything above
the middle layers, because they stay the wettest
every layer at exactly the same time as the others
the top layers, because they dry out in the sun

quiz.why_en: Over millions of years the bottom layers get squashed and turn into rock (WB p.40).

quiz.stem_en: Which sedimentary rock is formed from crushed sea shells?
quiz.why_en: Limestone is made from layers of shells of sea animals (p.72).

quiz.stem_en: A grey rock has very fine grains, leaves a mark when you scratch it and breaks in your hands. Which rock is it?
quiz.why_en: Shale is fine-grained, usually grey, and soft enough to scratch or break (p.72).

quiz.stem_en: How do the grains in sandstone compare with the grains in shale?

choices.en: both rocks have grains of the same size
sandstone has no grains at all

quiz.why_en: Sediments in sandstone are more coarse grained than in shale (WB p.40).

quiz.stem_en: What is a fossil?

choices.en: the preserved remains of an animal or plant in sedimentary rock
a crystal that grew as magma cooled down
a small piece of rock carried along by a river
a rock that heat and pressure have changed

quiz.why_en: Fossils are the preserved remains of animals and plants in sedimentary rocks (p.74).

quiz.stem_en: A dead leaf presses into soft mud that later hardens into rock. The leaf rots away, leaving a hollow print. What is this print called?
quiz.why_en: A mould is the imprint left behind in the sediments (p.75).

quiz.stem_en: A fossil can only form if the dead animal is buried quickly. What else must be true of the place where it is buried?

choices.en: the rock must already be hard
it must be close to a volcano
there must be very little air
the water must be boiling hot

quiz.why_en: A fossil only forms where the animal is buried quickly with very little air (p.74).

quiz.stem_en: What is a metamorphic rock?

choices.en: a rock made out of only one mineral
a rock formed from magma that cooled down
a rock made of sediments stuck together
an existing rock that heat or pressure has changed

quiz.why_en: Metamorphic rocks are existing rocks that have been changed (p.79).

quiz.stem_en: What happens to the minerals in a rock that is changed by heat?

choices.en: they melt and then form new crystals
they are washed away as sediments
they turn into air and disappear

quiz.why_en: When a rock is changed by heat all the minerals melt and then form new crystals (p.79).

quiz.stem_en: A rock is squeezed by huge pressure. What is the new rock like?

choices.en: it falls apart into sand grains
it has lots of thin layers
it has no crystals in it at all

quiz.why_en: Pressure squeezes the rock so much that the new rock has lots of thin layers (p.79).

quiz.stem_en: Where do the heat and the pressure that make metamorphic rock come from?

choices.en: sunlight warming the top of the ground
rain soaking down into the ground
a mass of magma forcing its way into the crust
wind blowing hard across the surface

quiz.why_en: Magma rises and forms an intrusive igneous mass, and the surrounding rocks are changed (p.79).

quiz.stem_en: Layers of sediment keep piling up on a sea bed. What happens to the bottom layer?

choices.en: it stays exactly the same for millions of years
it dries out and blows away as dust
it floats slowly up to the top of the pile
it is squashed by the layers above and can change into slate

quiz.why_en: Burial puts the bottom layer under huge pressure and changes it into slate (p.81).

quiz.stem_en: Which metamorphic rock forms when limestone is heated?
quiz.why_en: When limestone is heated it changes into marble (p.80).

quiz.stem_en: Which sedimentary rock does quartzite form from?
quiz.why_en: When sandstone is heated the sand grains melt and make quartzite (p.80).

quiz.stem_en: Slate splits into thin flat layers, which is why people use it for roof tiles. Which rock does slate form from?
quiz.why_en: Shale under intense pressure forms thin layers and becomes slate (p.81).

quiz.stem_en: A very hard rock has crystals like granite, but they lie in stripes or bands. Which rock is it?
quiz.why_en: Gneiss forms from granite, and pressure puts its crystals into bands (p.81).

quiz.stem_en: In the rock cycle, what has to happen to magma before igneous rock forms?
quiz.why_en: The blue arrow on the rock cycle shows magma cooling to form igneous rock (p.84).

quiz.stem_en: Which two actions break rock up into sediments?
quiz.why_en: The green arrows on the rock cycle are weathering and erosion (p.84).

quiz.stem_en: What are the two changes that can happen to a sedimentary rock in the rock cycle?

choices.en: it can be dissolved by rain or blown away by the wind
it can float to the surface or sink down to the mantle
it can be buried and changed, or weathered and eroded
it can be melted into magma or cooled into crystals

quiz.why_en: Sedimentary rock can become metamorphic rock, or break down into sediments (p.85).

quiz.stem_en: What is soil made of?

choices.en: melted rock that cooled down slowly
the shells of dead sea animals
broken-up rock, organic matter, water and air

quiz.why_en: Soil is a mixture of broken up rocks, organic matter, water and air (p.88).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these counts as organic matter in a soil?
quiz.why_en: Organic matter is living things or things which were alive, such as dead leaves (p.88).

quiz.stem_en: What does the word texture describe about a soil?

choices.en: how it feels when you rub it
how heavy a bucket of it is

quiz.why_en: Texture is the feel of a material, for example rough or smooth (p.88).

quiz.stem_en: Sandstone and quartzite weather into which kind of soil?
quiz.why_en: Sandstone and quartzite weather into sandy soil (p.89).

quiz.stem_en: A soil feels smooth and sticky, cracks in dry weather and will not let water drain away. Which soil is it?
quiz.why_en: Clay soil is smooth and sticky, cracks when dry and can become waterlogged (p.90).

quiz.stem_en: What is loam?

choices.en: a soil with a balance of sand, clay and organic matter
a soil that is made of clay and nothing else
a soil with no organic matter in it at all
a soil made from crushed sea shells

quiz.why_en: Loam is a soil with a balance of sand, clay and organic matter (p.90).

quiz.stem_en: What does waterlogged mean?

choices.en: full of water that will not drain through

quiz.why_en: Waterlogged means full of water that will not drain through (p.90).

quiz.stem_en: A gardener has loam but wants soil that drains better. What can be added?
quiz.why_en: Adding sand to loam makes a sandy loam soil, which drains well (p.91).

quiz.stem_en: Why do farmers and gardeners dig or plough the soil?

choices.en: to kill all the worms in it
to mix air into the soil

quiz.why_en: Digging and ploughing mix air into the soil, which it needs (p.92).

quiz.stem_en: What is compost made from?
quiz.why_en: Compost is a natural fertiliser made from dead organic matter (p.92).

quiz.stem_en: Compost and artificial fertiliser both give a soil nutrients. What can compost do that artificial fertiliser cannot?

choices.en: improve the texture of the soil
kill the insects on the plants

quiz.why_en: Artificial fertilisers give the same nutrients but do not improve the texture (p.92).

quiz.stem_en: A farmer plants the same crop year after year. What happens to the soil?

choices.en: it turns from sandy soil into clay
it holds far more water than before
the nutrients are used up and it dries out easily
it slowly becomes darker and richer

quiz.why_en: The same crop uses up the nutrients, and the soil dries out and stops growing plants well (p.92).

quiz.stem_en: Pesticides kill unwanted insects. What else do they kill?

choices.en: the water held in the soil
the organic matter in the soil

quiz.why_en: The chemicals in pesticides also kill the organic matter in the soil (p.92).

quiz.stem_en: What do the arrows in a food chain show?

choices.en: the direction in which the food and its energy move
the direction in which the animals travel

quiz.why_en: The arrows show the direction the food moves, and because food contains energy they also show the direction energy is transferred (p.99).

quiz.stem_en: What does every food chain start with?
quiz.why_en: The order in a food chain is always producer → consumer (p.99).

quiz.stem_en: Why is energy always transferred from the producer to the consumer in a food chain?

choices.en: because the consumer eats the producer
because the producer eats the consumer
because consumers make their own food
because the producer is always bigger

quiz.why_en: Energy goes from the producer to the consumer because the consumer eats the producer (p.99).

quiz.stem_en: A corn plant, a mouse and a snake make one food chain. Which order is correct?
quiz.why_en: A food chain starts with the producer, the corn plant, and the arrows point towards the animal that eats: the mouse, then the snake (p.99).

quiz.stem_en: What is a food web?

choices.en: one line of animals that eat each other
a map of where animals live
a list of the producers in a habitat

quiz.why_en: Different food chains link together to form a food web (p.100).

quiz.stem_en: Why is a food web a more accurate way than a food chain to show how energy is transferred?

choices.en: it shows only the producers in a habitat
it uses fewer arrows than a food chain
it shows every food chain a living thing is part of
it shows how big each animal in the habitat is

quiz.why_en: Most animals eat more than one food, and a food web shows the different food chains a living thing can be part of in its habitat (p.100).

quiz.stem_en: In a rainforest, the orangutan eats palm shoots, figs, jack fruit and beetles, and it is eaten by tigers and pythons. What kind of consumer is the orangutan?
quiz.why_en: It eats both plants and an animal, the beetle, so it is the omnivore in the Indonesian rainforest food web (p.100-101).

quiz.stem_en: In an ocean, jelly fish eat plant plankton, sea turtles eat jelly fish and great white sharks eat sea turtles. Which living thing is the producer?
quiz.why_en: The chain is plant plankton → jelly fish → sea turtle → great white shark, and it starts with the producer (WB p.51).

quiz.stem_en: In the Namib Desert, termites eat bits of grass, spiders eat termites, lizards eat spiders and the sidewinder adder eats lizards. Which food chain is correct?

choices.en: sidewinder adder → lizard → spider → termite → grass
grass → termite → spider → lizard → sidewinder adder
termite → grass → spider → lizard → sidewinder adder
grass → spider → termite → lizard → sidewinder adder

quiz.why_en: The chain starts with the grass and each arrow points to the animal that eats the one before (WB p.53).

quiz.stem_en: Where do producers get their energy from?
quiz.why_en: Producers get their energy from the Sun and use it to make food (p.101).

quiz.stem_en: A herbivore gets energy from the plants it eats. Which of these does NOT happen to that energy?

choices.en: all of it is passed on to the carnivore that eats the herbivore
some is used by the herbivore to stay alive
some is stored in the herbivore's body
some is transferred to the surroundings as heat

quiz.why_en: A carnivore only gets the energy stored in the herbivore's body; the rest is lost from the food chain (p.102).

quiz.stem_en: In the food chain bean plant → grasshopper → lizard → hawk, which living thing receives the least energy from the chain?
quiz.why_en: Energy is lost at each link, so the amount transferred gets less and less towards the end of the chain (p.102).

quiz.stem_en: What are microplastics?

choices.en: tiny plants that live in the sea

quiz.why_en: Microplastics are very small particles of plastic, and they can be toxic in ocean food chains (p.104).

quiz.stem_en: What does 'toxic' mean?
quiz.why_en: Toxic means harmful or poisonous, like mercury and cadmium are to living things (p.104).

quiz.stem_en: Why do farmers and gardeners use pesticides?

choices.en: to get rid of pests that eat their plants
to help the soil hold water

quiz.why_en: Farmers and gardeners use chemicals called pesticides to get rid of insects, snails, worms and other pests that eat their plants (p.105).

quiz.stem_en: Flowers are sprayed with a pesticide, and butterflies that drink their nectar die. What does this show?

choices.en: pesticides can kill consumers that are not pests

quiz.why_en: Pesticides can also kill consumers in a food web that are not pests, such as butterflies (p.105).

quiz.stem_en: A bird eats a snail that was killed by a pesticide, and a wildcat later eats the bird. What happens to the pesticide?

choices.en: it is destroyed inside the dead snail
it enters the bird, and the wildcat takes in what is still in the bird
it stays only in the bird and never reaches the wildcat
it turns into energy for the wildcat

quiz.why_en: The pesticide enters the bird's body, and a predator that eats the bird takes in any pesticide still in it (p.105).

quiz.stem_en: A toxic substance does not break down in the environment. Which living things in a food chain does it harm most?

choices.en: the predators at the end of the chain

quiz.why_en: Substances that do not break down accumulate in food chains and especially harm the predators at the end (p.106).

quiz.stem_en: A bug takes in 5 units of pesticide. A lizard eats 3 of these bugs, and an eagle eats 2 of these lizards. How many units of pesticide does the eagle take in?
quiz.why_en: The lizard gets 3 × 5 = 15 units and the eagle gets 2 × 15 = 30 units (p.106).

quiz.stem_en: In a game, green algae held 2 toxic particles, a shrimp 8 and a small fish 24. A big fish ate five small fish. How many toxic particles did the big fish take in?
quiz.why_en: Each small fish held 24 particles, so five of them give 5 × 24 = 120 (p.111 Q2).

quiz.stem_en: A factory dumps a harmful chemical into a river. Pond weed ends up with 4 units, a tadpole 20, a fish 240 and a heron 500. What pattern do these numbers show?

choices.en: the chemical breaks down along the food chain
the further along the food chain, the more chemical a living thing holds
the producer holds the most chemical
every living thing holds the same amount

quiz.why_en: The chemical builds up from 4 units in the pond weed to 500 in the heron at the end of the chain (WB p.56).

quiz.stem_en: Why can the pesticide DDT move through food chains?

choices.en: animals' bodies cannot get rid of it
only plants can take it in

quiz.why_en: DDT moves through food chains because animals' bodies cannot get rid of it; it is stored mainly in body fat (WB p.57).

quiz.stem_en: Which statement about harmful substances in food chains is true?

choices.en: they always break down in the soil
they move through food chains instead of energy
people can take them in by eating plants or animals that contain them

quiz.why_en: Humans who eat plants or animals that contain DDT are more likely to develop cancer and other serious diseases (WB p.57).

quiz.stem_en: What is mass?

choices.en: the amount of matter in an object
the pull of gravity on an object
the force needed to lift an object
the space an object takes up

quiz.why_en: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (p.113).

quiz.stem_en: Which unit is used to measure weight?
quiz.why_en: Scientists measure weight in newtons (N) (p.113).

quiz.stem_en: An astronaut travels from the Earth to the Moon. What happens to his mass and his weight?

choices.en: his mass stays the same and his weight gets smaller
his weight stays the same and his mass gets smaller

quiz.why_en: Mass is the same wherever you are, but the Moon's weaker gravity makes you weigh less (p.113).

quiz.stem_en: Why is the Moon's gravity weaker than the Earth's?

choices.en: the Moon is further from the Sun
the Moon is colder than the Earth
the Moon has a smaller mass than the Earth

quiz.why_en: The amount of gravity depends on mass, and the Moon has a smaller mass than the Earth (p.113).

quiz.stem_en: Which instrument measures weight in newtons?
quiz.why_en: Weight is measured in newtons on a forcemeter (p.114).

quiz.stem_en: A nurse says a newborn baby weighs 3.6 kg. What should she have said to be scientifically correct?
quiz.why_en: An amount in kilograms is a mass; weight is measured in newtons (p.113-114).

quiz.stem_en: A man has a mass of 90 kg on Earth. He travels to a planet where gravity is only half as strong. What is his mass on that planet?
quiz.why_en: Mass stays the same wherever an object is; only the weight changes with gravity (WB p.62).

quiz.stem_en: On Earth, a brick with a mass of 1 kg has a weight of 10 N. What is the weight of a 10 kg bag of potatoes on Earth?
quiz.why_en: Each kilogram has a weight of 10 N on Earth, so 10 kg weighs 100 N (WB p.61).

quiz.stem_en: Why do astronauts float inside the International Space Station?

choices.en: they are not pulled in any particular direction
there is no air inside the station

quiz.why_en: The station's forward motion about equals its fall, so the astronauts inside are not pulled any particular way and float (p.116).

quiz.stem_en: Why do astronauts in space have to exercise for two hours every day?

choices.en: to keep warm in the cold of space
to stop the station from falling

quiz.why_en: Astronauts' muscles become weak in space, so they exercise to try to overcome this (p.117).

quiz.stem_en: What happens to astronauts' bones after weeks or months in space?
quiz.why_en: Calcium in their bones is lost through their urine, which weakens the bones (p.117).

quiz.stem_en: Why does pulling down on an object hanging from a forcemeter give a wrong reading of its weight?

choices.en: the object loses some of its mass
you are adding to the weight

quiz.why_en: Pulling adds your own force to the weight, so the reading is too high (WB p.61).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these can a force do to an object?

choices.en: change what it is made of

quiz.why_en: A force can change an object's shape or size, start or stop it, or make it go faster or slower (p.120).

quiz.stem_en: A ping pong ball rests on a table. You blow on it through a straw. What effect does the force have?
quiz.why_en: A force can make an object at rest start to move (p.120-121).

quiz.stem_en: A rolling ball runs into a book standing up at the end of a table. What does this force do to the ball?
quiz.why_en: One effect of a force is to stop a moving object (p.121).

quiz.stem_en: A ball is rolled across a table covered with a cloth instead of across the bare table. What effect does the cloth have on the ball?

choices.en: it makes the ball go faster
it makes the ball go round in circles
it slows the moving ball down

quiz.why_en: The ball rolls more slowly on the cloth: a force can slow down a moving object (p.120-121).

quiz.stem_en: You gently press down on a ping pong ball that is resting on a table. What does the force do?

choices.en: changes the shape of the ball

quiz.why_en: Pressing on the ball is a force that changes its shape (p.121).

quiz.stem_en: What does a force diagram show?

choices.en: the mass of an object in kilograms
the name, size and direction of the forces on an object
the order in which things happen

quiz.why_en: Force diagrams show the name, size and direction of forces acting on an object (p.119).

quiz.stem_en: A girl pedals her bike faster. What is the effect of the force?

choices.en: it changes the shape of the bike
it changes the direction of the bike
it changes the speed of the bike

quiz.why_en: Pedalling faster changes the speed of the bike (WB p.63).

quiz.stem_en: A player hits a tennis ball back over the net. What is the main effect of the force on the ball?

choices.en: it changes the colour of the ball
it stops the ball for good
it changes the direction of the moving ball

quiz.why_en: Hitting the ball back changes the direction of a moving object (WB p.64).

quiz.stem_en: A tennis ball is rolled across a strip of sandpaper on the floor. Which effect of a force does this show?

choices.en: changing the shape of an object
changing the mass of an object

quiz.why_en: The sandpaper slows down the moving tennis ball (WB p.67).

quiz.stem_en: A soccer ball is resting on the ground. Which forces act on it?

choices.en: upthrust from the air and friction
gravity and the ground pushing up
no forces, because it is not moving

quiz.why_en: A resting ball still has two forces on it: gravity pulling down and the normal force of the ground pushing up (WB p.67).

quiz.stem_en: Which two forces act on an object on water?

choices.en: weight due to gravity and upthrust

quiz.why_en: When an object is on water, its weight due to gravity and upthrust act on it (p.125).

quiz.stem_en: You push a ball down on to the surface of water and feel the water pushing up underneath it. What is this force called?
quiz.why_en: The water pushing up underneath the ball is the upthrust force (p.125).

quiz.stem_en: When will an object float?

choices.en: when its mass is less than or equal to the mass of water it displaces
only when it is made of plastic
when its mass is greater than the mass of water it displaces
only when it is very small

quiz.why_en: An object floats if its mass is less than, or equal to, the mass of water displaced by upthrust (p.125).

quiz.stem_en: On a force diagram of a ball in water, the gravity arrow is longer than the upthrust arrow. What happens to the ball?

choices.en: it rises out of the water
it stays still at the surface

quiz.why_en: When the gravity arrow is longer than the upthrust arrow, the ball sinks below the surface (p.126).

quiz.stem_en: A container ship has a mass of thousands of tons. Why does it float?

choices.en: all its containers are full of air
it displaces an even greater mass of water than its own mass
ships have no weight at sea

quiz.why_en: The ship has a huge mass but displaces an even greater mass of water, so it floats (p.126).

quiz.stem_en: Sand is added 10 g at a time to a small plastic container floating on water. What finally happens?

choices.en: it sinks once enough sand has been added

quiz.why_en: Adding sand increases the container's mass until it is greater than the mass of water displaced, and it sinks (p.126).

quiz.stem_en: Coins of 5 g each are added one at a time to a polystyrene raft floating in a glass container of water, until it sinks. What is the independent variable?

choices.en: the number of coins on the raft
whether the raft floats or sinks

quiz.why_en: The number of coins is what is changed; floating or sinking is what is observed (WB p.70).

quiz.stem_en: A polystyrene raft floats with six coins on it but sinks when a seventh coin is added. Why does it sink?

choices.en: the coins make the water colder
the mass of the raft and coins is now more than the mass of water displaced
the upthrust is now bigger than gravity
the raft soaks up the water

quiz.why_en: The raft sinks when the mass of the raft and coins is more than the mass of water displaced by upthrust (WB p.70).

quiz.stem_en: How could a polystyrene raft be changed so that it holds more coins before it sinks?
quiz.why_en: Making the raft wider or longer increases its area, so it can carry more coins (WB p.70).

quiz.stem_en: Foil containers were loaded with coins until they sank. A 2 cm² base held 1 coin, 7 cm² held 3, 11 cm² held 6 and 16 cm² held 9. What trend would a scatter graph show?

choices.en: a trend that goes down and then up

quiz.why_en: As the base area goes up the number of coins also goes up, which is a positive trend (p.128, p.173).

quiz.stem_en: Apart from mass, what else affects whether an object floats or sinks?
quiz.why_en: Mass is not the only thing that affects floating and sinking; shape does too (p.127).

quiz.stem_en: A submarine opens its ballast tanks and lets water in where there was air. Why does it sink?

choices.en: the water makes the upthrust bigger
its total mass becomes more than the mass of water it displaces
the water pushes it down from above

quiz.why_en: With the tanks full of water, the submarine's total mass is more than the mass of water it displaces (WB p.72-73).

quiz.stem_en: Why can people all over the world read circuit diagrams?

choices.en: they are always drawn in colour
they have instructions written in English
they show photographs of the components

quiz.why_en: Circuit symbols are conventional: they are used by everybody (p.131).

quiz.stem_en: Which symbol stands for a motor in a circuit diagram?

choices.en: a circle with a cross inside
two dots joined by a line
a circle with the letter M inside

quiz.why_en: The motor symbol is a circle with the letter M inside (p.131).

quiz.stem_en: Which symbol stands for a bulb in a circuit diagram?

choices.en: a circle with a cross inside
a circle with the letter M inside
a line with a gap and a tilted part
a long line beside a short thick line

quiz.why_en: A bulb is drawn as a circle with a cross inside (p.131).

quiz.stem_en: A 3 V buzzer is put into a circuit. What does it need to make it work?
quiz.why_en: A 3 V buzzer needs a 3 V battery to make it work (p.133).

quiz.stem_en: How can you make a 3 V battery?

choices.en: join a lamp to a 1.5 V cell

quiz.why_en: You can make a 3 V battery by joining two 1.5 V cells (p.133).

quiz.stem_en: A circuit has a 3 V battery, a buzzer, connecting wire and an open switch. Why does the buzzer not sound?

choices.en: a buzzer needs a 1.5 V cell
the open switch breaks the circuit

quiz.why_en: An open switch breaks the circuit, so the buzzer will not work (WB p.75).

quiz.stem_en: In a series circuit, how many paths does the electric current have?
quiz.why_en: In a series circuit the electric current has only one path (p.134).

quiz.stem_en: One lamp in a string of festival lamps connected in series stops working. What happens?

choices.en: the other lamps shine more brightly
none of the lamps light up
only the lamps next to it go out

quiz.why_en: If one lamp in a series string does not work, none of the lamps will light up (p.134).

quiz.stem_en: Why do the other lamps in a parallel circuit stay alight when one lamp burns out?

choices.en: each lamp has its own circuit with the battery

quiz.why_en: In a parallel circuit each lamp has its own circuit with the battery (p.135).

quiz.stem_en: Two identical lamps are joined to the same 3 V battery, once in series and once in parallel. In which circuit do the lamps shine more brightly, and why?

choices.en: series, because the current has only one path
series, because the lamps share the battery
parallel, because the lamps are closer together
parallel, because the full strength of the battery goes to each lamp

quiz.why_en: In a parallel circuit the full strength of the battery goes to each lamp, so they shine more brightly (WB p.76).

quiz.stem_en: A circuit has lamps 1 and 2 in series on one path, and lamp 3 on its own separate path to the same battery. Which lamp shines brightest?
quiz.why_en: Lamps 1 and 2 share the electricity, but lamp 3 gets the full strength (WB p.77).

quiz.stem_en: Light reflects off a plane mirror. How does the angle it leaves at compare with the angle it arrives at?
quiz.why_en: Light reflects from a mirror at the same angle as it arrives (p.144).

quiz.stem_en: Which surface is best at reflecting light?

choices.en: a piece of dull black cloth

quiz.why_en: Smooth, polished surfaces, like mirrors, are very good at reflecting light (p.143).

quiz.stem_en: What is the ray of light that arrives at a mirror called?
quiz.why_en: The arriving ray of light is called the incident ray (p.144).

quiz.stem_en: What is the normal in a ray diagram?

choices.en: the ray that bounces off the mirror
a line drawn at right angles (90°) to the surface of the mirror
the angle between the two rays
the shiny surface of the mirror

quiz.why_en: The normal is a line drawn at right angles (90°) to the surface of the mirror (p.144).

quiz.stem_en: A flamingo stands in a clear, still lake. What do you see in the water below it?

choices.en: nothing, because water cannot reflect light
the flamingo's real legs under the water
a dark shadow with no shape
the mirror image of the flamingo

quiz.why_en: Clear, still water reflects light well, so you see the mirror image of the flamingo (p.143).

quiz.stem_en: When you see your face in a plane mirror, what are you seeing?

choices.en: light made inside the glass of the mirror
light passing through the mirror from behind it
light from your face reflecting off the mirror
your shadow falling on the mirror

quiz.why_en: You are seeing light from your face reflecting off the mirror (p.143).

quiz.stem_en: An incident ray makes an angle of 40° with the normal of a plane mirror. What angle does the reflected ray make with the normal?
quiz.why_en: The angles that each ray makes with the normal are the same (p.144).

quiz.stem_en: What is a periscope?

choices.en: a device that uses mirrors to let you see things that are otherwise out of sight
a lens that makes far-away things look bigger and nearer to you
a glass prism that splits white light into the colours of the rainbow
a tube that makes light travel faster so you can see in the dark

quiz.why_en: A periscope uses plane mirrors and reflection so you can see things out of sight (p.146).

quiz.stem_en: At what angle are the mirrors set inside a periscope?
quiz.why_en: The lines for the mirrors are drawn at 45° to the horizontal (p.147, p.166).

quiz.stem_en: A man inside a submarine under the water is using a periscope. What is he most likely using it for?

choices.en: to make the water around the submarine clearer
to light up the inside of the submarine
to see what is above the surface of the water
to measure how deep the water is

quiz.why_en: A periscope lets you see things that are otherwise out of sight (WB p.82, p.146).

quiz.stem_en: Which way do the two mirrors of a periscope face?

choices.en: the top one faces up and the bottom one faces down
the top one faces down and the bottom one faces up

quiz.why_en: The top mirror has its reflecting surface facing down and the bottom mirror facing up (p.147).

quiz.stem_en: Light from a person on the other side of a wall enters a periscope. Which path does it take to your eyes?

choices.en: top mirror, down the periscope, bottom mirror, then your eyes
bottom mirror, up the periscope, top mirror, then your eyes
straight through both mirrors without changing direction
top mirror, then straight into your eyes without reaching the bottom mirror

quiz.why_en: Light reflects off the top mirror, travels down to the bottom mirror and reflects into your eyes (p.148).

quiz.stem_en: What is refraction?

choices.en: the bouncing of light off a mirror
the blocking of light by a solid object
the making of light by the Sun

quiz.why_en: Refraction is the bending of light (p.150).

quiz.stem_en: Why does light bend when it passes from water into air?

choices.en: the air pushes the light upwards
it travels at different speeds through different mediums
the water soaks up part of the light
it reflects off the surface of the water

quiz.why_en: Refraction occurs because light travels at different speeds through different mediums (p.150).

quiz.stem_en: A pencil stands in a glass of water. Seen from the side, it looks bent. Why?

choices.en: the water soaks into the wood and makes the pencil soft and bendy
its light refracts as it passes out of the water and glass into the air
the curved glass reflects the pencil twice, like two mirrors
the pencil casts a bent shadow on the water in the glass

quiz.why_en: Light from the pencil bends as it passes from the water through the glass to the air (p.151, WB p.82).

quiz.stem_en: You look at a fish in a pond. Where is the fish really?

choices.en: exactly in the straight line from your eyes where it seems to be
just above the surface of the water
nowhere, because it is only a reflection
in a different place from where it seems to be

quiz.why_en: The light from the fish refracts, so seeing it in a direct line from your eyes is an optical illusion (p.150).

quiz.stem_en: A stone lies at the bottom of a container of water. How does it look to someone peering in from above?

choices.en: nearer the surface than it really is

quiz.why_en: Because of refraction the stone appears to be nearer the surface than it really is (p.166).

quiz.stem_en: What is a lens?

choices.en: a transparent material with at least one curved surface
a line drawn at 90° to a mirror

quiz.why_en: A lens is a transparent substance with at least one curved surface (p.151).

quiz.stem_en: What does a convex lens do to the light rays passing through it?

choices.en: it bends them outward so they spread apart
it bends them inward so they meet at the focal point

quiz.why_en: Light rays bend inward through a convex lens and converge at the focal point (p.152, WB p.83).

quiz.stem_en: A drop of water sits on plastic wrap laid over a newspaper. What does the drop do to the words under it?

choices.en: it splits them into seven colours
it makes them look bigger, because the drop acts as a convex lens
it makes them look smaller, because the drop is a mirror

quiz.why_en: The water drop magnifies the words; you have made a lens (p.152).

quiz.stem_en: What type of lenses are used in binoculars?
quiz.why_en: Convex lenses are used to make binoculars (p.152, WB p.84).

quiz.stem_en: What happens when a narrow ray of white light passes through a prism?

choices.en: it refracts and splits into different colours

quiz.why_en: The ray refracts and splits into different colours (p.153).

quiz.stem_en: When can you see a rainbow?

choices.en: when it is sunny and raining, with the Sun behind you and the rain in front
when the Sun is in front of you and the rain behind you

quiz.why_en: It has to be sunny and raining at the same time, with the Sun behind you and the rain in front (p.153).

quiz.stem_en: In a rainbow, what acts like tiny prisms?
quiz.why_en: The raindrops act like tiny prisms (p.154).

quiz.stem_en: The Sun is about 500 times larger than the Moon. Why do they look about the same size to us?

choices.en: the Moon gives out more light
they are really the same size
the Sun is much further away from us

quiz.why_en: The Sun is about 150 million km away and the Moon only 390 000 km (p.156).

quiz.stem_en: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
quiz.why_en: Mercury is 60 million km from the Sun, the closest of the eight planets (p.156).

quiz.stem_en: In a model of the Solar System the Sun is a tennis ball, Mercury is a grain of sugar 3 m away and Neptune is a lentil 250 m away. What does this model show that an ordinary diagram cannot?

choices.en: how far apart the planets really are compared with their sizes
what each planet is made of
how long each planet takes to orbit
how many moons each planet has

quiz.why_en: An ordinary diagram is not to scale: to scale, Neptune would be a kilometre away from the Sun (p.156-157).

quiz.stem_en: How long does the Earth take to turn once on its axis?
quiz.why_en: The Earth turns on its axis once every 24 hours or day (p.159).

quiz.stem_en: Which planet turns on its axis in the opposite direction to most other planets?
quiz.why_en: Venus turns in the opposite direction to most other planets (p.160).

quiz.stem_en: Which planet has a moon that is larger than the planet Mercury?
quiz.why_en: Jupiter's biggest moon, Ganymede, is larger than Mercury (p.160, WB p.89).

quiz.stem_en: Mercury orbits the Sun in 88 Earth days, Earth in 365¼ days, Mars in 687 Earth days and Jupiter in 11.9 Earth years. What pattern do these numbers show?

choices.en: the further a planet is from the Sun, the longer it takes to orbit
every planet takes the same time to orbit
the closer a planet is to the Sun, the longer it takes to orbit

quiz.why_en: The planets are listed in order from the Sun, and their orbit times get longer each time (p.160, WB p.90).

quiz.stem_en: How long does the Moon take to complete its orbit around the Earth?
quiz.why_en: It takes 29.5 days for the Moon to orbit the Earth, which we call a month (p.161).

quiz.stem_en: Why do we sometimes see half the Moon and sometimes no Moon at all?

choices.en: the Earth's shadow covers a different part of the Moon each night
the Moon makes its own light only on some nights
only half of the Moon is lit by the Sun, and we see different amounts of that lit half
clouds always hide part of the Moon

quiz.why_en: Only half the Moon can be lit up by the Sun at any one time; the part of it we see is the phase (p.161).

quiz.stem_en: What is the phase called when the whole side of the Moon facing us is lit up?
quiz.why_en: At full Moon the whole of the Moon facing us is lit up, so we see a circle (p.163).

quiz.stem_en: The lit-up part of the Moon looks larger every night. What is the Moon doing?
quiz.why_en: When the Moon appears larger every night we say it is waxing (p.163).

quiz.stem_en: Tonight there is a full Moon. Which phase comes next?
quiz.why_en: After full Moon (E) the Moon moves to the gibbous position F and starts to wane (p.162-163).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'The heart pumps air around the body.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Wrong — the heart pumps blood; air goes in and out of the lungs.
Right — the heart pumps air to every part of the body.
Right — the heart pumps air, and the veins carry it.
Wrong — the heart pumps food, and the lungs pump air.

quiz.why_en: The heart is a muscle whose job is to pump blood through the body (p.3, p.33).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'The veins carry blood to all parts of the body.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — veins carry blood from the heart to every body part.
Wrong — arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins bring it back.
