Right — veins and arteries both carry blood away from the heart.
Wrong — capillaries carry all the blood away from the heart.

quiz.why_en: Arteries carry blood away from the heart to the body, and veins carry it back towards the heart (p.5, p.33).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'When you breathe in, your chest gets smaller.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — the chest gets smaller to squeeze air into the lungs.
Right — the ribs move down and in when you breathe in.
Wrong — breathing in makes the chest bigger as the lungs fill with air.
Wrong — the chest stays the same size while you breathe.

quiz.why_en: When you breathe in, the ribs move up and out and the chest gets bigger, so the lungs fill with air (p.14).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'When you breathe out, your chest gets bigger.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — the chest gets bigger to make room for the air leaving.
Right — the diaphragm moves down, so the chest gets bigger.
Wrong — the chest gets bigger only when you exercise.
Wrong — the chest gets smaller, and that pushes air out of the lungs.

quiz.why_en: When you breathe out, the diaphragm relaxes and moves up and the chest gets smaller, pushing air out (p.14).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'Only boys grow more hair on their bodies during puberty.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Wrong — both boys and girls grow more body hair in puberty.
Right — girls do not grow any new hair during puberty.
Right — more body hair is a sign that only boys get.
Wrong — only girls grow more hair during puberty.

quiz.why_en: In puberty hair grows in the armpits and other parts of the body in both boys and girls (p.20; WB p.11).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'During menstruation, a male sex cell and a female sex cell join.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — menstruation is when a sperm and an egg join.
Wrong — that is fertilisation; menstruation releases an unfertilised egg.
Right — menstruation is when new eggs are first formed.
Wrong — in menstruation, two eggs join together.

quiz.why_en: In menstruation an unfertilised egg leaves the body with the lining of the uterus; the joining of sex cells is fertilisation (p.21; WB p.11).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'All infectious diseases are caused by viruses.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — viruses are the only living things that cause diseases.
Right — bacteria and fungi are always harmless.
Wrong — bacteria, fungi and other parasites cause diseases too.
Wrong — all infectious diseases are caused by bacteria.

quiz.why_en: Bacteria cause cholera, fungi cause athlete's foot, and other parasites cause malaria (p.25; WB p.14).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'Living things that spread diseases always get the disease themselves.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — a mosquito can only spread malaria it has caught.
Right — vectors always die of the disease they spread.
Wrong — living things that spread diseases never bite people.
Wrong — a mosquito spreads malaria but does not get the disease.

quiz.why_en: Insects that spread a disease do not get the disease themselves, so we call them vectors (p.29; WB p.14).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'Evaporation only happens at the boiling point.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Wrong — evaporation can happen at any temperature, at the surface.
Right — a liquid must boil before any of it can evaporate.
Right — evaporation and boiling are the same process.

quiz.why_en: Most liquids boil only when heated, but evaporation of surface particles can happen at any temperature (p.36; LMS: Unit 2 study guide).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'If you heat more of a substance, its melting point will be higher.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — a bigger amount always melts at a higher temperature.
Wrong — the melting point is a property, so the amount does not change it.
Right — a smaller amount melts at a higher temperature.
Wrong — heating more of it makes its melting point lower.

quiz.why_en: Melting point is a property of a substance, so each substance has its own melting point (p.36, p.38).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'Saucepan handles are made of plastic because plastic is a good conductor of heat.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — the plastic handle carries heat quickly to the food.
Right — plastic conducts heat better than the metal pan.
Wrong — plastic is a poor conductor of heat, so the handle stays cool.
Wrong — plastic handles are used because plastic conducts electricity.

quiz.why_en: Non-metals such as plastic are not good conductors of heat, which is why pan handles are made from plastic (p.44-45; LMS: Unit 2 study guide).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'Electrical wires are covered in plastic because plastic conducts electricity well.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — the plastic carries the electricity along the wire.
Right — plastic conducts electricity better than copper.
Wrong — the plastic is there because it conducts heat well.
Wrong — plastic is an electrical insulator, so it keeps the current in the metal.

quiz.why_en: Plastic, rubber and glass are electrical insulators: they are not good conductors of electricity (p.61; LMS: Unit 2 study guide).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'Evaporation is irreversible because the water disappears.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Wrong — the water becomes water vapour, and condensation turns it back into water.
Right — once water evaporates, it is gone for ever.
Right — evaporation turns water into a new substance.
Wrong — evaporation is reversible because the water freezes.

quiz.why_en: Evaporation and condensation can be reversed: water turns into water vapour and back into water (LMS: Unit 2 study guide; p.50).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'Dissolving salt in water is an irreversible change.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — the salt turns into water when it dissolves.
Wrong — dissolving is reversible: the salt is still there in the water.
Right — you can never get dissolved salt back.
Wrong — dissolving is reversible because salt melts in water.

quiz.why_en: Dissolving salt in water is a reversible change: sea water is salty because the salt is still in the water (p.51; WB p.28).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'When cooking gas burns in oxygen, heat is one of the reactants.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — heat, gas and oxygen are all reactants.
Right — heat is the product and also a reactant.
Wrong — heat is not a substance; the reactants are cooking gas and oxygen.
Wrong — water is one of the reactants in this reaction.

quiz.why_en: Reactants are the substances that react; cooking gas and oxygen react to form carbon dioxide and water (p.57; WB p.34).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'When magnesium burns in oxygen, the bright white flame is the product.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — a flame is a new substance made in the reaction.
Right — the flame and the oxygen are both products.
Wrong — the oxygen is the product of the reaction.
Wrong — the white powder is the product; the flame is evidence of the reaction.

quiz.why_en: Products are new substances; the white powder is new, while the flame only shows that a reaction took place (p.57-58; WB p.34).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'Shiny black beach stones on a volcanic island, with crystals too small to see, are granite.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Wrong — tiny crystals mean lava cooled fast, so the stones are basalt.
Right — all black shiny stones near a volcano are granite.
Right — granite forms when lava cools at the surface.
Wrong — they are sandstone, because they are on a beach.

quiz.why_en: Lava from a volcano cools quickly at the surface into basalt, whose crystals are too small to see (p.65-66; WB p.39).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'The magma that made granite cooled down quickly.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — that is why granite crystals are too small to see.
Wrong — it cooled slowly deep in the crust, so its crystals are big.
Right — granite formed from lava at the Earth's surface.
Wrong — granite formed from sediments, not from magma.

quiz.why_en: Magma deep in the crust cools slowly, so granite has crystals large enough to see (p.65-67).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'Fossils are only found in sandstone.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — sandstone is the only rock that can hold fossils.
Right — fossils only form in hard igneous rocks.
Wrong — fossils are found in all kinds of sedimentary rock.
Wrong — fossils are only found in metamorphic rock.

quiz.why_en: Fossils are found only in sedimentary rocks, such as sandstone, shale and limestone (p.74; WB p.40).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'Heat and ice break up rocks in a process called erosion.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — breaking up rock where it lies is erosion.
Right — erosion and weathering are the same process.
Wrong — that process is called sedimentation.
Wrong — that is weathering; erosion then wears the rock down into sediments.

quiz.why_en: Weathering breaks rock up where it lies; erosion by rivers, ice and wind wears it down into sediments (p.71; WB p.40).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'Metamorphic rocks form when magma cools and becomes rock.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Wrong — that makes igneous rock; metamorphic rock is existing rock changed.
Right — all rocks made from cooled magma are metamorphic.
Right — metamorphic rocks form from cooling lava only.
Wrong — metamorphic rocks form when sediments build up.

quiz.why_en: Metamorphic rocks are existing rocks changed by heat, pressure or both; cooled magma makes igneous rock (p.65, p.79; WB p.43).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'Metamorphic rocks are very soft.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — heat and pressure make rocks soft and crumbly.
Wrong — they are very hard, like marble and quartzite.
Right — metamorphic rocks break easily in your hands.
Wrong — metamorphic rocks are soft only when wet.

quiz.why_en: Heat and pressure make harder rock: quartzite is much harder than sandstone, and marble is extremely hard (p.80; WB p.43).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'All the particles in a soil are the same size.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — every soil has particles of exactly one size.
Right — sand and clay particles are the same size.
Wrong — loam has particles of different sizes, and soils differ in size.
Wrong — soil has no particles, only organic matter.

quiz.why_en: Sandy soil has large particles, clay soil very small ones, and loam a mixture of different sizes (p.89-90).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'Pesticides only kill unwanted insects, so they cannot harm the soil.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — pesticides make the soil better for plants.
Right — pesticides only change the colour of the soil.
Wrong — pesticides harm soil because they add too much water.
Wrong — pesticides also kill the organic matter in the soil.

quiz.why_en: A pesticide kills unwanted insects but also kills the organic matter in the soil (p.92, p.95).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'Each animal eats only one kind of food, so it belongs to only one food chain.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Wrong — most animals eat more than one kind of food.
Right — every animal has just one kind of food.
Right — a frog eats only flies, so it is in one chain.
Wrong — animals eat only plants, never other animals.

quiz.why_en: Most animals eat more than one kind of food, so they belong to more than one food chain (p.100).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'All the energy in the food a consumer eats is passed on to the next link.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — energy is never lost along a food chain.
Wrong — only part of it is passed on; the rest is used or lost.
Right — each link gets more energy than the one before.
Wrong — none of the energy is ever passed on.

quiz.why_en: Not all the energy in the food a consumer eats is passed on, so less reaches each next link (p.102).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'Harmful substances move through food chains instead of energy.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — once toxins get in, energy stops moving.
Right — toxins take the place of energy in food.
Wrong — they move along with the food, and energy is still passed on.
Wrong — harmful substances cannot move through food chains.

quiz.why_en: A pesticide moves along a food chain each time one living thing eats another, together with the food and its energy (p.105; WB p.56).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'Harmful substances in food chains cannot affect humans.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — toxins only harm the animals at the end.
Right — humans are not part of any food chain.
Wrong — they affect humans only by touching the skin.
Wrong — people who eat affected plants or animals can be harmed.

quiz.why_en: People who eat plants or animals containing a pesticide such as DDT are more likely to get serious diseases (WB p.56-57).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'Mass and weight are the same.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Wrong — mass is the matter in kg; weight is gravity's pull in newtons.
Right — both are measured in kilograms.
Right — both change when you go to the Moon.
Wrong — mass is a force and weight is matter.

quiz.why_en: Mass is the amount of matter in kilograms, and weight is the pull of gravity in newtons (p.113; WB p.61).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'An astronaut has less mass on the Moon than on Earth.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — weaker gravity makes the mass smaller.
Wrong — the mass stays the same; only the weight is less.
Right — both mass and weight are less on the Moon.
Wrong — the astronaut has more mass on the Moon.

quiz.why_en: An object has the same mass wherever it is, but weaker gravity on the Moon gives it less weight (p.113-114).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'A ball resting on a table has no forces acting on it.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — forces only act on objects that are moving.
Right — a force only acts when you push the ball.
Wrong — forces act on objects at rest too, such as gravity pulling it down.
Wrong — only one force can act on a ball at a time.

quiz.why_en: Forces act on objects at rest as well as moving ones; gravity and the push of the ground act on a resting ball (p.119; WB p.67).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'Forces can make things move, but they cannot change an object's shape.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — forces only start or stop movement.
Right — only heat can change an object's shape.
Wrong — forces change shape but cannot make things move.
Wrong — a force can change shape, as when you crack an egg.

quiz.why_en: Forces can make an object move, slow it down, stop it, change its direction or change its shape (p.121; WB p.63).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'A huge container ship is so heavy that it should sink.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Wrong — it displaces a mass of water greater than its own mass.
Right — a ship floats only because it is moving.
Right — heavy objects always sink in water.
Wrong — ships float because water has no gravity.

quiz.why_en: A container ship floats because it displaces an even greater mass of water than its own huge mass (p.124, p.126).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'Only the mass of an object decides whether it floats or sinks.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — shape never changes whether an object floats.
Wrong — its shape matters too, as foil containers of different sizes show.
Right — only very light objects can ever float.
Wrong — only the colour of an object decides it.

quiz.why_en: Mass is not the only thing that affects floating and sinking; the shape of the object matters too (p.127-128).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'If one lamp in a series circuit does not work, the other lamps still light up.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — each lamp in a series circuit has its own path.
Right — the other lamps shine even more brightly.
Wrong — the current has only one path, so none of the lamps light.
Wrong — only the lamp next to the battery goes out.

quiz.why_en: In a series circuit, if one lamp does not work, none of the lamps will light up (p.134).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'If one lamp in a parallel circuit burns out, all the other lamps go out.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — all lamps share one path in a parallel circuit.
Right — a parallel circuit works just like a series circuit.
Wrong — only the lamps on the left side go out.
Wrong — each lamp has its own circuit, so the rest stay alight.

quiz.why_en: In a parallel circuit each lamp has its own circuit with the battery, so if one burns out the rest stay alight (p.135).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'Light leaves a mirror at a bigger angle than it arrives.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Wrong — light leaves a mirror at the same angle as it arrives.
Right — the reflected angle is always bigger.
Right — the reflected angle is always twice as big.
Wrong — light leaves at a smaller angle than it arrives.

quiz.why_en: The incident ray and the reflected ray make the same angle with the normal (p.144, p.146).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'In a periscope, the top mirror faces up and the bottom mirror faces down.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — that sends the light out of the top of the tube.
Wrong — the top mirror faces down and the bottom mirror faces up.
Right — both mirrors must face the same way.
Wrong — both mirrors must face straight ahead.

quiz.why_en: The top mirror faces down and the bottom mirror faces up, so light reflects down the tube and into your eyes (p.147-148).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'A pencil in a glass of water looks bent because of reflection.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — the water acts like a mirror for the pencil.
Right — the glass reflects the pencil into a new shape.
Wrong — it is refraction: light bends as it passes from water to air.
Wrong — the water really bends the pencil.

quiz.why_en: The pencil looks bent because light refracts, or bends, as it travels from one medium into another (p.150; WB p.82).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'A convex lens makes things look smaller because light rays bend outwards.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — convex lenses are used to make things smaller.
Right — light rays spread out and never meet.
Wrong — it makes things bigger because rays go straight.
Wrong — it makes things look bigger, because the rays bend inwards.

quiz.why_en: A convex lens makes things look bigger: its light rays bend inwards and converge at the focal point (p.152; WB p.83).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'The Earth moves around the Moon.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Wrong — the Moon orbits the Earth, once every 29.5 days.
Right — the Earth orbits the Moon once a month.
Right — the Earth and the Moon do not move at all.
Wrong — the Moon orbits the Sun, not the Earth.

quiz.why_en: The Moon takes 29.5 days to orbit the Earth, and we call this a month (p.155, p.161).

quiz.stem_en: A student says, 'The Sun and the Moon are about the same size, because they look the same size.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Right — things always look as big as they really are.
Wrong — the Sun is about 500 times larger but much further away.
Right — the Moon is a little bigger than the Sun.
Wrong — the Moon is 500 times larger than the Sun.

quiz.why_en: The Sun is about 500 times larger than the Moon but looks the same size because it is much further away (p.156).

quiz.stem_en: Which type of scientific enquiry do we use when an investigation would be impossible or unsafe to do?
quiz.why_en: When an investigation is impossible or unsafe, we do research in books, on the internet or in videos (p.viii).

quiz.stem_en: Books, the internet and videos are called what kind of information?
quiz.why_en: Books, the internet and videos are secondary sources of information (p.viii).

quiz.stem_en: Pupils want to know which factors, apart from exercise, affect pulse rate. They look in books and on the internet and report back. Which type of enquiry is this?
quiz.why_en: Finding the answer in books and on the internet is research (p.10, p.viii).

quiz.stem_en: A student says: 'We can find out how the coronavirus is spread by doing a fair test in class.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Correct, because a fair test answers every science question
Not correct, because such a test is unsafe, so we use research
Correct, because viruses are easy to see in class
Not correct, because pattern seeking uses a key

quiz.why_en: How the coronavirus is spread is found out by research, the enquiry we use when a test is impossible or unsafe (p.viii).

quiz.stem_en: Pupils want to see how the shape of the Moon changes as it orbits the Earth. For about how long must they keep observing?
quiz.why_en: We need a month to observe the changes in the Moon's appearance as it orbits the Earth (p.ix).

quiz.stem_en: Salt crystals are left to grow on a paperclip hanging in a jar of salt solution, and the jar is checked every day for a week. Which type of enquiry is this?
quiz.why_en: Checking the jar every day for a week to see the crystals grow is observing over time (p.68, p.ix).

quiz.stem_en: Which change can be seen straight away, WITHOUT waiting?

choices.en: the Moon changing shape as it orbits the Earth
salt crystals growing on a paperclip in a jar
an iron nail rusting in a saucer of water
a gas forming when vinegar and baking soda are mixed

quiz.why_en: The gas forms straight away when vinegar and baking soda are mixed; the Moon's changes take a month (p.ix).

quiz.stem_en: What do we use to sort things into groups by asking a series of 'yes or no' questions?
quiz.why_en: We can classify things by asking a series of 'yes or no' questions, for example with a key (p.x).

quiz.stem_en: How can we identify whether a blood vessel is an artery, a vein or a capillary?

choices.en: by counting the pulse for one minute
by measuring how fast the heart beats
by features we recognise, such as the thickness of its wall
by doing a fair test on blood

quiz.why_en: We name blood vessels because they have features we recognise, such as the thickness of the wall (p.x).

quiz.stem_en: A pupil sorts a collection of rocks into igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks by looking at how they are different. Which type of enquiry is this?
quiz.why_en: We classify materials into groups by observing the ways in which they are different (p.x, p.64).

quiz.stem_en: Why do scientists often use pattern seeking to study things in nature?

choices.en: The variables in nature cannot easily be controlled.
Nature is always too dangerous to study.
Patterns can only be found in a laboratory.

quiz.why_en: We often find patterns in nature, where we cannot easily control the variables (p.x).

quiz.stem_en: Pupils measure the mass and the weight of many different objects and look for a link between the two sets of readings. Which type of enquiry is this?
quiz.why_en: Measuring mass and weight and looking for the link between them is pattern seeking (p.112, p.x).

quiz.stem_en: In a fair test, how many variables do we change?
quiz.why_en: In a fair test we change one variable and keep all the others the same (p.viii).

quiz.stem_en: What is the variable that we change in a fair test called?
quiz.why_en: The independent variable is the one that we change (p.viii).

quiz.stem_en: What do we call the variables that we keep the same in a fair test?
quiz.why_en: The variables that we keep the same are the control variables (p.ix).

quiz.stem_en: A teaspoon of sugar is stirred into 100 ml of cold water and into 100 ml of hot water, and the time it takes to dissolve is measured. What is the dependent variable?

choices.en: the time the sugar takes to dissolve

quiz.why_en: The time it takes the solute to dissolve is the dependent variable that we measure (p.ix, p.54).

quiz.stem_en: Sugar is timed as it dissolves in hot water and in cold water. Why must both jars have 100 ml of water and one teaspoon of sugar?

choices.en: so that only the water temperature can affect the result
so that the sugar dissolves faster
so that the water stays hot for longer
so that the test takes less time

quiz.why_en: Changing only one variable means no other variable can affect the results (p.viii).

quiz.stem_en: Sugar is timed as it dissolves in water at 20 °C, 40 °C, 60 °C and 80 °C. What is the independent variable?

choices.en: the time for the sugar to dissolve

quiz.why_en: The water temperature is changed on purpose, so it is the independent variable (WB p.31-32, p.viii).

quiz.stem_en: Sand is added 10 g at a time to a small plastic container floating on water, until it sinks. What is the independent variable?

choices.en: whether the container floats or sinks
the amount of water in the large container
the mass of sand in the container
the size of the plastic container

quiz.why_en: The mass of sand is what is changed each time, so it is the independent variable; floating or sinking is observed (p.126).

quiz.stem_en: Sand is added 10 g at a time to a small plastic container floating on water, until it sinks. Which is a control variable?

choices.en: using the same plastic container every time
the prediction written down each time

quiz.why_en: The same container and the same water are kept the same; only the sand changes (p.126, p.ix).

quiz.stem_en: A student tests copper, aluminium, plastic and rubber in a circuit with a battery, wires and a bulb, to see whether the bulb lights. Which variable does the student change?
quiz.why_en: The material is changed on purpose; whether the bulb lights is what is observed (LMS: Unit 2 Study Guide).

quiz.stem_en: A student tests which materials conduct electricity by putting each one into a circuit with a bulb. Why should the same battery be used every time?

choices.en: so that only the material can change whether the bulb lights
so that the bulb lights more brightly
so that the battery lasts longer
so that the wires do not get hot

quiz.why_en: Keeping the battery the same means no other variable affects the result (LMS: Unit 2 Study Guide, p.viii).

quiz.stem_en: A student puts pieces of chocolate in different places to see where they melt. What should be kept the same to make it a fair test?

choices.en: the place where each piece is put
the size of each piece of chocolate

quiz.why_en: The place is what is changed, so everything else, such as the size of each piece, must stay the same (LMS: Unit 2 Study Guide).

quiz.stem_en: Equal blobs of petroleum jelly hold beads on a metal spoon, a plastic spoon, a glass rod and a pencil, all in one beaker of hot water. A student says: 'This is a fair test.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Not correct, because the materials are all different
Not correct, because the water is hot
Correct, because only the material changes and the rest stays the same
Correct, because every bead falls off at the same time

quiz.why_en: Only the material is changed; the jelly, beads and hot water are kept the same (p.43, p.viii).

quiz.stem_en: Water, olive oil and vinegar are heated to find out which one turns into a gas first. Which things must be kept the same for a fair test?

choices.en: the type of liquid being heated
the boiling point of each liquid
the amount of liquid, the burner and the heating time
which liquid turns into a gas first

quiz.why_en: 100 ml of each liquid is heated on the same burner for the same time; only the liquid changes (WB p.21).

quiz.stem_en: Pupils plan a fair test on how exercise affects pulse rate. What do they do first?

choices.en: draw a bar chart of the results
make a prediction and say why
work out the average pulse rate

quiz.why_en: The plan starts with a prediction and the reason for it (p.9).

quiz.stem_en: Pupils plan a test to compare the boiling points of different liquids. Which question helps them to work safely?

choices.en: Are there any dangers or risks, and how will we avoid them?
Which liquid do we like best?
How many colours will the graph have?

quiz.why_en: The plan asks what dangers or risks there are and how to work safely (p.38).

quiz.stem_en: Pupils make salt crystals using jars of very hot salt water. What is the risk in this activity?

choices.en: burning yourself on the very hot water

quiz.why_en: The activity involves handling very hot water, so be careful not to burn yourself (p.68).

quiz.stem_en: What should a good prediction include?

choices.en: a reason for what you think will happen

quiz.why_en: Make a prediction and say why you made it (p.9).

quiz.stem_en: What should you use to make a prediction?

choices.en: what you already know about science

quiz.why_en: We use scientific knowledge to make a prediction (p.35).

quiz.stem_en: Sand is added 10 g at a time to a small container floating on water. When should you write down whether you think it will float or sink?
quiz.why_en: A float or sink prediction is written in the table before each 10 g of sand is tested (p.126).

quiz.stem_en: Sugar is stirred into hot water and into cold water. Which prediction uses science knowledge?

choices.en: It will dissolve faster in hot water, because the particles move faster.
It will dissolve faster in cold water, because cold water is fresher.
It will take the same time, because both are water.
It will not dissolve in hot water, because heat destroys sugar.

quiz.why_en: Heat gives the particles more energy, so they move faster and the solute dissolves faster (p.54).

quiz.stem_en: Hot salt solution is left to form crystals, one jar in a warm place and one in a fridge. Magma that cools slowly forms large crystals. Which prediction uses this?

choices.en: The jar in the warm place will make bigger crystals, because it cools slowly.
The jar in the fridge will make bigger crystals, because it cools faster.
Both jars will make crystals of exactly the same size.
Neither jar will make crystals, because salt only dissolves.

quiz.why_en: Slow cooling makes large crystals (p.66), so the jar that cools slowly should make the bigger crystals (p.68).

quiz.stem_en: A graph shows how well some substances conduct heat and electricity. How can you predict the heat value of a new substance whose electricity value is 14?

choices.en: take the average of all the heat values
use the value of the best conductor
read it off the graph at 14 on the electricity axis

quiz.why_en: The graph is used to predict the heat measurement for a substance with an electricity value of 14 (p.47).

quiz.stem_en: A pupil predicted the bead on the plastic spoon would fall off first, but the bead on the metal spoon fell off first. What should the pupil say?

choices.en: The prediction was correct, because a bead fell off.
The result is wrong, because it does not match the prediction.
The prediction was not correct, because the result was different.
The spoons must be swapped until the prediction is right.

quiz.why_en: Results are used to say whether a prediction was correct; here it was not (p.44).

quiz.stem_en: A pupil predicts a pencil in a glass of water will look straight. Seen from the side, it appears to bend. Was the prediction correct?

choices.en: Correct, because the pencil is straight when taken out
Not correct, because the pencil appeared to bend
Not correct, because the water changed the pencil's shape

quiz.why_en: The pencil appears to bend in the water, so the prediction did not match what was seen; out of the water it is unchanged (p.150-151).

quiz.stem_en: Pupils predict that adding another cell will make a buzzer louder. They test it. What should they do next?

choices.en: change the results to match the prediction
check whether the evidence supports their prediction
write a new prediction without testing
stop, because a prediction is always right

quiz.why_en: After making each circuit, ask whether the evidence supports your predictions (p.133).

quiz.stem_en: A student predicts that plastic will conduct electricity. When plastic is put in the circuit, the bulb does not light. What does this show?

choices.en: The prediction was wrong: plastic does not conduct electricity.
The prediction was right, because the bulb is new.
Plastic conducts electricity, so the bulb must be broken.
Plastic conducts a little, so the bulb is dim.

quiz.why_en: The bulb does not light, so plastic does not conduct electricity and the prediction was not accurate (LMS: Unit 2 Study Guide).

quiz.stem_en: Pupils measure the mass and the weight of several objects. Which columns should their results table have?

choices.en: mass in newtons, weight in grams
object, mass in grams, weight in newtons

quiz.why_en: The table needs a column for the objects, one for mass in grams and one for weight in newtons (p.115).

quiz.stem_en: Lamp brightness is recorded with ticks: no ticks, one tick or two ticks. What do two ticks mean?
quiz.why_en: 0 ticks: the lamp does not shine; 1 tick: dim; 2 ticks: bright (p.46).

quiz.stem_en: Pupils add sand 10 g at a time to a floating container and predict each time whether it will float or sink. Which headings should their table have?

choices.en: amount of water, colour of sand, result

quiz.why_en: The three columns are Amount of sand, Prediction (float or sink) and Result (float or sink) (p.126).

quiz.stem_en: A pupil counts breaths per minute at rest, after running on the spot and while resting again. Which graph does the pupil draw?
quiz.why_en: The breathing rate results are drawn as a line graph (p.16).

quiz.stem_en: The melting points of three different solids are measured. A student says: 'A line graph is the best way to show these results.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Not correct, a bar chart with one bar per solid is used
Correct, because a line graph joins the three solids
Correct, because melting points always make a line
Not correct, a scatter graph with no axes is used

quiz.why_en: The melting points of the three solids are drawn as a bar chart (p.38).

quiz.stem_en: Learners act as rice plants, caterpillars, frogs and kingfishers collecting paper 'pesticide' particles. The average for each living thing is graphed. Which kind of graph is used?
quiz.why_en: A bar graph shows the average number of particles found in each type of living thing (p.107).

quiz.stem_en: When do we use a scatter graph?

choices.en: when we measure only one thing
when we sort rocks into groups
when we expect a trend between two sets of data

quiz.why_en: We use a scatter graph to present two sets of data when we think there is a trend between them (p.170).

quiz.stem_en: Why is a line of best fit drawn on a scatter graph?

choices.en: to join every dot in order
to give the graph a heading
to make the trend more obvious
to hide results that do not fit

quiz.why_en: A line of best fit is drawn through the dots to make the trend more obvious (p.172).

quiz.stem_en: On a scatter graph, as one value increases the other value decreases. What kind of trend is this?
quiz.why_en: When one value increases and the other decreases, the graph shows a negative trend (p.173).

quiz.stem_en: The dots on a scatter graph are spread all over, and no line of best fit can be drawn. What does this show?
quiz.why_en: When the dots are scattered and no line of best fit can be drawn, there is no trend (p.173).

quiz.stem_en: Weekly records: at 26 °C, 0 learners were off sick; at 20 °C, 3; at 14 °C, 8; at 10 °C, 16. What would a scatter graph of this show?

choices.en: a negative trend: more learners are sick when it is colder
a positive trend: fewer learners are sick when it is colder
no trend, because the dots are scattered
a positive trend, because both numbers go up

quiz.why_en: As the temperature decreases, sickness increases: a negative trend (p.171-173).

quiz.stem_en: After jogging, ten people's breathing rates and pulse rates are measured. People who breathe faster mostly have higher pulse rates. What trend is this?
quiz.why_en: When one value goes up and the other also goes up, it is a positive trend (WB p.8-9, p.173).

quiz.stem_en: Pulse rates before and after three minutes of exercise: pupil A 91 and 120, B 88 and 122, C 90 and 128, D 89 and 125. Whose pulse rate went up the most?
quiz.why_en: C went up by 38 beats, D by 36, B by 34 and A by 29 (p.33).

quiz.stem_en: Toxic particles taken in: green algae 2, shrimp 8, small fish 24. What pattern do these results show?

choices.en: the amount goes down at each step of the food chain
the amount goes up at each step of the food chain
every living thing takes in the same amount
the numbers go up and down with no order

quiz.why_en: The number of toxic particles is bigger at each link: 2, then 8, then 24 (p.111).

quiz.stem_en: A pupil's heartbeats per minute: sitting still 72, digging in the garden 80, riding a bicycle 110, running on the spot 120, playing football 150. What pattern do they show?

choices.en: the pulse rate is the same for every activity
the more active the pupil, the higher the pulse rate
the pulse rate is highest when sitting still
the pulse rate goes down during exercise

quiz.why_en: Sitting still gives the lowest rate and playing football the highest (WB p.4-5).

quiz.stem_en: Breathing rate and pulse rate of five people after jogging: 30 and 90, 32 and 95, 26 and 100, 38 and 106, 42 and 112. Which result does NOT fit the pattern?
quiz.why_en: Faster breathing goes with a higher pulse, but the slowest breather has a higher pulse than two faster ones (WB p.8-9).

quiz.stem_en: What should you do with a measurement that does NOT fit the pattern of the other results?

choices.en: change it so that it fits
copy the result next to it

quiz.why_en: If a measurement does not fit the pattern, repeat it (p.115, p.118).

quiz.stem_en: Why is your pulse counted three times rather than once?

choices.en: to make the heart beat faster
to make the result more reliable

quiz.why_en: Repeating measurements gives more reliable data; the three counts are used to work out an average (p.7-8, p.112).

quiz.stem_en: A thin ray of light is shone at a mirror from several angles, and the reflected ray is observed each time. Why is it a good idea to repeat this several times?

choices.en: to turn the mirror into a lens
to be sure the pattern is the same every time
to make the ray of light thinner

quiz.why_en: Observations are repeated to give more reliable data (p.142, p.146).

quiz.stem_en: A substance is placed between two wire ends in a lamp circuit, and the lamp does not light up. What should you do before recording the result?

choices.en: record that the lamp is bright
test the substance again to be sure
use a brighter lamp without testing
leave the substance out of the table

quiz.why_en: If the lamp does not light up, test the substance again to be sure of your result (p.46).

quiz.stem_en: William Harvey spent many hours repeating his experiments on the heart. Why do scientists repeat experiments?

choices.en: to check that their results are reliable
to make the experiment last longer
to get a different answer each time
so they do not need a conclusion

quiz.why_en: Harvey was very thorough and repeated his experiments (p.31); repeating gives more reliable data (p.112).

quiz.stem_en: Groups test different lengths of graphite in a circuit and score the lamp's brightness from 0 to 5. Why is an average brightness worked out for each length?

choices.en: to change the length of graphite
to make the graph look neater
to make the results more reliable

quiz.why_en: Using the average of several groups' results makes the data more reliable (WB p.26-27, p.112).

quiz.stem_en: What is a conclusion?

choices.en: what you think will happen before the test
the list of equipment you need
what you found out in the investigation

quiz.why_en: A conclusion is what you found out in the investigation (p.38).

quiz.stem_en: A bulb lights when copper is put in the circuit, but not when plastic is. What can the student conclude?

choices.en: Plastic conducts electricity and copper does not.
Both copper and plastic conduct electricity.
Copper conducts electricity and plastic does not.
Neither copper nor plastic conducts electricity.

quiz.why_en: The bulb only lights when the material lets electricity through (LMS: Unit 2 Study Guide).

quiz.stem_en: The teacher heats three solids until each melts and measures the temperature. A student says: 'If we heated more of each solid, the melting points would change.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Correct, because more solid melts at a higher temperature
Not correct, because the melting point is a property of the substance
Correct, because a bigger amount melts at a lower temperature
Not correct, because solids never melt

quiz.why_en: The temperature at which a substance changes state is a property of the substance, so the amount does not change it (p.35, p.38).

quiz.stem_en: A student melts some chocolate and then leaves it to cool. What evidence would show that this change is reversible?

choices.en: The chocolate turns into a gas.
The chocolate burns and turns black.

quiz.why_en: The chocolate can melt and then become solid again when it cools (LMS: Unit 2 Study Guide).

quiz.stem_en: A student says: 'Evaporation is irreversible because the water disappears.' Is the student correct?

choices.en: Not correct, because water vapour can condense back into water
Correct, because the water is gone for ever
Correct, because evaporation makes a new substance
Not correct, because evaporation only happens at 100 °C

quiz.why_en: Evaporation and condensation can be reversed: water → water vapour → water (LMS: Unit 2 Study Guide).

quiz.stem_en: Why do scientists use models?

choices.en: to make their results more reliable
to keep the control variables the same
to describe and understand things they cannot see

quiz.why_en: Scientists use models to describe and understand things they cannot see (p.168).

quiz.stem_en: Which of these is a model?

choices.en: a pulse rate of 90 beats a minute
a diagram of the circulatory system

quiz.why_en: Diagrams are models; we use them to describe what body systems look like (p.168).

quiz.stem_en: What does a 3D model of the heart show well?

choices.en: how fast the heart beats after exercise
the size of the heart and what it looks like inside
the pulse rate of a pupil
the order in which the blood vessels were discovered

quiz.why_en: A 3D model gives a good idea of the size of body systems and what they look like inside (p.168).

quiz.stem_en: Why is a globe a good model of the Earth?

choices.en: It is exactly the same size as the Earth.
It has the right shape and tilt, and turning it shows night and day.
It shows every person living on the Earth.
It shows what is deep inside the Earth.

quiz.why_en: A globe is the correct shape, tilted at the correct angle, and turns to explain night and day (p.169).

quiz.stem_en: Which kind of model makes it easiest to understand how the planets move in orbits?

choices.en: a moving model with a lamp as the Sun
a scale model of planets on sticks in a field
a table of the planets' sizes

quiz.why_en: To understand how everything moves in orbits it is much easier to have a moving model (p.170).

quiz.stem_en: A scale model of the Solar System is set out in a field. What does it NOT show well?

choices.en: how big the Sun is compared with the planets
how far apart the planets are
that the small planets are closest to the Sun
how the planets move in their orbits

quiz.why_en: A scale model shows sizes and distances; a moving model is needed to show orbits (p.170).

quiz.stem_en: A model of breathing has a balloon on a straw inside a plastic bottle, and a stretched balloon across the bottle's cut-off bottom. What does the stretched balloon represent?
quiz.why_en: Pulling the bottom balloon works like the diaphragm muscle moving down (p.15).

quiz.stem_en: How do circuit diagrams help us?

choices.en: They make the lamp shine brighter.
They measure the voltage of the battery.
They help describe a circuit and understand how it works.
They stop the current from flowing.

quiz.why_en: Circuit diagrams are models that help describe a circuit and understand how it works (p.169).

quiz.stem_en: Why do we need models to study the Solar System?

choices.en: it is much too small to see clearly
we can only see a tiny part of it at any one time
it stays still, so there is nothing to watch
it is hidden deep inside the Earth

quiz.why_en: We cannot see the Solar System except through a powerful telescope, and even then only a tiny part of it (p.169).
